SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview of
Red Norvo
Conducted by Helen Dance

New York, New York
May 2, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
Would you just say something into the mike now?
All right, is it getting it?

Yeah, I think it is. You speak -- Okay, this is Red Norvo and this Helen Vance talking with Red Norvo and I've asked him to start right at the beginning and we're going to start from scratch and see where we go to.
Well, I was born March 31st, 1908, and in Beardstown, Cass County, Illinois.
Beardstown, what? et sic
Beardstown --
Yeah?
In Cass County --
Cass County, is that C-a-s-s?
That's Cass County --
Yeah --
It's in the State of Illinois.
Yeah --
It's on the Illinois River.
I'm a foreigner, you know, so --
It's on the Illinois River --
Yeah.
Just about -- above St. Louis.
Good.
The Illinois River meets Mississippi at St. Louis --
Oh --
-- just above St. Louis.
Is that -- well that's not -- is that South? I mean in the sense is it southern country or it's real -- I mean --
Not, it's just southern Illinois. Southern Illinois.
Okay, yeah. Well all right, Red, what kind of population --
The town is about --
Like that --
-- about, Oh I think at that time it was a railroad town, so it probably up around eight - 10,000.
Oh.
But, it's diminished since then. Except I was back last year -- it's a nice town -- it's on the River.
Really?
And course we have the usual problems as a kid with -- when I was a child that River would overflow and had levees around the town --
Oh, yeah.
Which would -- finally after the rainy season they would -- they'd have to fix them every year. If
they didn't break in the one year they would hope they would hold the following year, one of these things.
Yeah.
So it was always a thing in the Spring of the year --
Yeah.
You didn't know.
Yeah. So -- do you remember any -- any circumstance when the water came in and so on?
Oh, yeah, sure.
Really?
Well, sure, that's -- my goodness the town was flooded, it was -- you could row a boat through the whole town?
Really?
Oh, yeah. Sure. It would come up -- luckily the house that I lived in was high enough, it didn't get in --
Oh.
-- but it's in the basements of all the houses --
Oh. And --
The house on either side of us, had about six inches on the first floor --
Oh.
So we were quite lucky. It came up to about six inches below the floor --
Gee.
It was such a mess --
Ah -- it must be appalling.
-- afterward, such dirt and everything.
Must be terrible.
But -- it is --
Yeah.
-- cause you have no heat you see, you have furnaces in the basement --
Oh, yeah.
And --
Oh, so with the flood --
Yeah, you don't have no heat -- it's pretty miserable.
Does it wreck the furnace?
Does it what?
Does it wreck the furnace, altogether? I mean, afterwards?
No, not altogether, but just takes -- it's the slime that you have to shovel out from the basements afterwards and everything and kind of a while --
Oh.
We had a room in the basement where my
mother used to put up fruit --
Oh, yeah.

-- and can things and they'd be floating around in the room, You'd see them -- look down in the basement you'd see it -- and they'd go through the stove, it didn't bother the stove too much. Course the coal was down there too --
Would the coal --
Most the time you had a boat if you went someplace and --
I mean would it last a couple of days?
Oh, my. Might last weeks. That's-- that's -- it could last weeks until the water went down. Might last six weeks.
Re-ally?
Sure, it was an awful mess when it went down.
So for six weeks there was no heat?
Yeah, sometimes maybe, three or four weeks.
Gosh.
Sometimes it wasn't too bad, maybe -- would just break in a certain section of the town and wouldn't cover the town --
No, would have been --
Since then they've built a wall -- the
-- and it's now surrounded by walls so --
Oh.
-- they don't have happen that condition anymore.
But what would it do to the electricity, wouldn't that get knocked out, too?
You'd have electricity, but maybe you wouldn't have gas.
Oh.
Not only that, if you had a coal -- like we had -- our kitchen stove was an old range -- coal range stove, with -- with an oven --
Yeah?
-- my mother used to bake --
I remember, yeah.
So that was a problem.
Yeah.
Cause you didn't have electric stoves or gas stoves then --
No.
See?
Yeah.
Usually you prepared when you think it was going to happen.
Yeah. I mean is that -- is it usually winters or _-- I mean -- oh --
Oh, Spring --
Spring. Spring, yeah.
When it thaws and the rainy season --
Yeah.
-- which was April and if it was a snowy winter or --
Yeah.
-- a lot of snow, or a lot of rain --
-- Yeah.
-- in the Spring. It probably hit the end of April --
Yeah, you could know that you're going to expect it.
So when I'd read about the towns around the country being flooded, I realize what's happening.
Yeah, I mean, you know, down there in Florida we were really thinking about -- ,
Well, it's a nice little town,my father was a railroader, he worked for the Burlington. Night chief dispatcher and then the night chief --
Uh-huh.
And --
Does that --
What?
Does he always have to be away at nights then?
Yes, he was at nights. He worked -- let's see, from 12:00 to 8:00 for awhile. Different hours --
Yeah, yeah.
-- you know they had three shifts and those things.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
But there was a lot of coal going through. See the coal mines down in Herrin [Illinois] and lot of tra --
Yeah, yeah.
-- railroad traffic in those days.
Oh.
I had two brothers, and a sister, the oldest was Hoard, next was Glenn, and my sister was named Portia. I was the youngest.
Oh, you named your daughter after your sister, then.
Well my wife named her after --
Oh, how nice -- because I thought it was, you know --
Yeah, she liked the name so she wanted to name her --
So you were the youngest?
I was the young --
Of the four?
Of the four, yes I was the youngest.
Oh, how -- what.
They were two and a half years apart and I think I was six or eight years -- between my sister and I.
Yeah, I see. Oh, yeah. So your older (unintelligible) brother was quite a bit older.

I know my brothers were in college -- oh yeah they were in college when I was quite young, I know. Cause that's where I started to play, actually. Where I got interested in music is my hometown was flooded --
Yeah?
-- one year and my father sent my mother and my sister and I down to Missouri, where my brothers were in school, Rolla, Missouri --
Oh, I see.
-- Missouri School of Mines where they were going to school down there. And, so there was nothing to do , just hang around this little town --
Yeah?
-- I used to go to the theater at night. And there was a fellow by the name of Wentworth that played the marimba in the theater, they had a little band.
Yeah?
And I think it was a dime or something to go to the theaters, in those days --
Yeah?
So, I'd get that front seat everynight. And it was just something to -- fun to watch the band --
How old were you?
Oh, I don't know. I really don't remember how old I was then.
Well like --
Something like that.
Yeah, yeah.

And so one night he came up to the railing, I had the first seat on the aisle by his thing, he said, "You know you seem interested in that." He said, "You know I belong to the same fraternity as your brother, older brother." He said, "I have one in my room there, if you're doing nothing in the daytime, you know the keyboard?" I said, "Well, I know the -- I know the --" he said, "It's the same as the piano." I said, -- "You know that?" I said, "Yeah." He said, "well I have one up in my room," he said, "I'll leave some mallets on the instrument," he said, "and if you got nothing to do in the afternoon," he said, "There's nobody there, go on up and
That's nice --
--"monkey around with it." Yeah, piddle around.
Yeah.
So I did. And I got doing it more and more.
Well, explain to me about the marimba, just tell me how it is.
Well he had a little xylophone up in his room --
Yeah, oh.
But he had a marimba in the pit, quite a big instrument.
Yeah.
And he played well, I enjoyed watching him. And he played four hammers on the thing, and that was nice.
No kidding. And does it have pedals and so --
No, no, no. That's a vibra-harp.
Oh, I see.
That's a vibra-harp.
Yeah, I see.
You had to roll to lock -- it's played very different, you see.
Oh, yeah.
The vibra-harp is a -- well actually the first vibra-harp was without a pedal.
Was it?
Oh, sure, cause I used to play them behind strings with Victor Young where you'd hit the -- hit the notes -- hit the chords --
Yes.
Behind the strings and then you --
Oh.
-- if it was a half note or a, a note six beats you'd count up and then put your arms down on it.
Oh, really?
To stop the notes. Oh, sure. This is originally, before they had the pedal. It was really a glorified glockenspiel, was what --
Oh.
-- what the vibra-harp came out of. Was the glockenspiel.
Is that right.
But they put a motor on it, which made it have a vibrato --
Yeah.
And --
Yeah.
-- was up in string sections, like the downbeat, you know?
Yeah.
Victor Young used it very well --
Yeah.
-- at the Goldkette Band --
Yeah.
-- in Chicago --
Yeah, I want -- well we'll get to that, but I wanted to ask you about that, I knew that you were with Victor Young and so I want to ask you about that so --
I was there.
-- so let's -- well go on back, now.
But then the pedal is -- is well I was at NBC when the first pedal come on, in Chicago. And they started playing and then you could stop it with a pedal.
Yeah.
Everybody was complaining about the arm --
Yeah.
-- so they got the idea for the pedal.
Yeah, yeah. Were there --
Pardon?
-- were there many people using them then? Many people playing them then, at that time?
Oh, yeah, sure --
When the -- when the pedals --
Oh, they were very well known.
Yeah.
Lot of people -- xylophone players were using them.
Yeah.
Lot of people -- Al Fresco had one on the -- he was a vaudeville act, he had one --
Yeah.
-- he had a band on the stage, he used a vibra-harp.
OH.
He used it on the stage.
Yeah. Yeah.
Lot of guys played them.
Yeah.
Of course in those days when -- well I played xylophone, everybody wanted me to play xylophone.
Yeah.
Like Victor said, well use that for the violins, but when will you improvise, stay with the wood, it's a better sound --
Yeah, yeah.
-- I like the sound better. And it was that way with Whiteman, he wanted me to [do that.]
Yeah, yeah. Well when -- let me get you right back to where we -- started from. We're jumping here.
Pick up the threads.
Yeah. Well so -- so did you spend three or four weeks or something there? When you?
Yeah, I think we were there -- I don't know exact time.
Did you -- had you studied any piano, I mean did you know your chords or you -- you could read a little bit?
No, I didn't know chords, I couldn't read I didn't know notes. I just knew the piano. I'd taken about maybe six or 12 lessons. When I was about six years old. My brothers and sisters all played.
Oh.
My brother --
Your brothers?
Oh, yeah. My oldest brother was a pianist. And --
Where did it -- who was musical? Your mother or your father?
They're both. My mother was a trumpet player.
Was she?
She was a trumpet player in a girls' band.
No kidding?
Yeah.
That was exceptional in those days?
And --
-- did she get a pretty tone?
I don't know. I never heard her.
Didn't you?
I have a picture of her though, with the trumpet --
No kidding --
-- I still have it, I adore the picture and --
How about that?
And my father used to chord, you know, and sing with the piano --
Yeah.
What they call chording --
Yeah, yeah.
-- in those days, he could follow anybody, any key -- he'd follow --
Really?
Yeah, but my second brother was really the most -- probably the greatest talent, he was a great violinist. He had a lot of scholarships offered him and he won a lot of things, but --
Really?
-- he was also a football player.
For heaven's sake.
And it kind of broke my father's heart and said that's for sissies, not for football players and he wouldn't play anymore.
Oh, what a shame, eh?
My sister was always -- played piano and everything. She -- she graduated in music. She was a college-aholic, I think. She just kept always going to college.
Oh, really?
Oh, yeah. And she taught school --
Did she teach music, you mean?
Well, she taught regular school, then she she played organ --
Oh.
All these things, so --
Well that was --

-- it's strange cause my mother would always say, she couldn't improvise a note, but she could play anything, all these powerful Bach things --, when I'd go home I'd ask her -- we'd go over to the church and she'd play on that organ, and she had a Hammond organ at the house. So my mother used to laugh said if she could play at the skating rink and play jazz, like you do, she'd be the happiest person in the world.
Oh, isn't that funny, she minded that
she couldn't improvise.
Yeah, she knew so much music, and knew all about it, and yet she couldn't -- she used to say how do you do it, I'd say, I don't know, Portia, I really don't know.
Isn't that something. And of course --
Yeah?
-- the -- the violin ist -- I suppose something that -- with violin music I -- I mean would he improvise or did he even --
No, I don't remember that, I was rather young when he played --
Yeah, yeah.
-- then he went off --I know I was quite young when he went off to college.
Yeah, yeah.
And --
Yeah.

-- I don't remember too much about that -- at that time I was one of the kids that played out. I took about 12 lessons and she found out that I was playing by ear, and she hit me on the hands with a ruler, so I never wanted to go back, and I was so young, about six, that --
Yeah.
My mother was never one to force us to do anything --
Yeah -- yeah.
-- like that. And she said, well, if he wants bad enough he'll get it.
Well did you have a Hammond organ in the house in the beginning or did you --
Did I have what?
A Hammond organ in the house or did your sister --
No, no, no. That was after when I used to go home --
--get it later?
I mean after I was out of town.
YEAH, I see right.
And she acquired it --
Yeah, yeah.
-- she got her degree in music -- and
Yeah, yeah.
-- and --
Well when you went back home --
When I went from Rolla, back home I kept yearning for that. So I asked my dad to get one. And he wouldn't he said no. I think he was disappointed in my brother's stopping the violin.
Yeah.
And I don't think he thought I had anything
-- I didn't show too much, I think, in his mind that would warrant him going out and spending the money. So I had a pony --
yeah.
So I sold the pony, I got a $100.00. It was a Shetland, nice Shetland pony and I sold it and --
How did you have the pony -- when did you get the pony?
Well, we had it -- it was my older brothers, and then when he went to college he said, he came back one summer and I was taking care of it and he'd gone to college and --
Yeah.

So he said to me, I think you're big enough, he said, he was hitched out in front of the house. He said, I'm going to start in about 10 seconds and if you can ride him around -- tell me where to ride him, if you can ride him in so-and-so time, he's yours. And my mother was in the back and she looked up and here I had him wide open and she said, he's running with Ken, he's running away with Ken. She came running out in the front front lawn. And I pulled up in front of the house and he said, "No, I just told him he had to make it in so many seconds." So many minutes or something. And, so I made it so he said, I'm giving him the pony, so that's how I happened to have it. But I --
So you had to decide to part with the
Well I -- I never had a bicycle, I rode -- all I did was ride the pony -- I'd ride into town for groceries and get on, both arms and just ride --
Saddled? He was saddled?
Ah --
The pony had a saddle on?
Oh, yeah, I had a surrey too.
Oh, really?
Yeah had a two-cart surrey --
How about that?
-- I used to -- oh on Saturdays I'd go out to -- oh little town like Frederick and collect walnuts and things like that --
Yeah, yeah. And earn a little money, you mean, with it?
What?
Earn a little money with them, would you sell them?
I'd keep them myself.
OH, that was nice.
Walnuts -- black walnuts are beautiful.
Yeah.
In the wintertime, you know, in fudge, it's good --
Yeah.
-- cold weather -- course we had no radio or anything like that in those days.
No, that's right. Yeah. Had to make your own fun.
Read -- yeah there was no radio or television.
Did you have many pals around? Kids your own age, convenient?
Yeah, oh yeah.
Anybody else that was musical?
You mean in my neighborhood?
Yeah.
No.
No.

As I got a little older I met some. Course there was Mel Healt who was in that town and the Skinner boys, you know Frank Skinner. They -- he had the Ranger, he had three brothers that worked in Macedosia, which is right down the River a little ways --
Yeah?
And they used to come up all the time.
Did you -- didn't have radio, but what about phonograph. Did they have phonographs?
Yes, they had phonographs.
Well did your family have any records?
Yeah, they had records.
What kind of records?
Edison -- that's what --
Yeah, but -- yeah, but I mean --
-- big, thick Edison records.
But what were you listening to on them?
Ray Miller's orchestra.
Yeah, what else?
George Hamilton Green.
I don't remember that one.
He's a xylophone player.
Oh, really?
Yeah, when I came back I found out that he made Victor -- made Edison records.
Oh, so you got those.
Yeah. I had -- I got them --
Yeah.
-- I used to listen to them.
Yeah.
And he had an all-star trio. On Victor, too. You had a gadget where you could play the Edison and also the other kind, play the small kind, you know --
Oh --
Thin ones, --
Yeah.
It was different you needed a diamond point needle or something or other.
Oh, yeah yeah.
I don't remember too much about it.
Yeah, but that's how it was. Yeah.
And so I --
So --
-- I'd listen to the --
Yeah. Well anyway, so then you let the pony go --
Well I got $100.00 for that and then I worked on the railroad. I played with a couple -- I mean a couple of pals of mine, their father was on the railroaders, too --
Yeah.
So one of them was the head of the roundhouse there, and in the summertime a lot of the boys would get jobs with the railroad.
Doing what?
Oh, I was a pick-up gang. You know that we have to change the wheels underneath the boxcars --
OH? No kidding?
And the boxcars, they'd -- they'd repair the wood on the side --
Oh, yeah.
And they'd tear that off and put it back on and we'd have to pick that up and throw it in the or --
Yeah.
And bring the double wheels under, we didn't have -- had everything ground down.
Yeah.
And things like that.
So --
I think I saved -- I saved most of that. I think I had saved $38.50 or something and it was a -- enough to get a first one, which was a table-model.
Oh.
And I just monkeyed with it. I enjoyed just --
No lessons at all then, huh?
Not then. No I just monkeyed around with it. And later -- later --
So what would you --
-- later I found that'-- nobody taught, see there was no teachers in my town -- no music teachers, piano teacher. Nobody knew how to play that instrument.
Yeah.
There was nobody, I just got books and I listened to George Hamilton Green on records and --
Would you be using two mallets or -- what one?
Two mallets, yes.
Yeah.
And trying to get -- my mother would say well, you know, try and get it perfect, try and get it right, you know?
Yeah. She had that musical sense.
She said everytime you play it, try to do it better. Try do it --
Yeah, yeah.
So she kind of instilled in me the idea that --
Yeah.
-- she kind of perfected it -- good --
Yeah, I guess she was pleased to see that you --
Not -- they weren't -- nobody paid much mind to it.
Yeah, it's funny isn't it --

Then after -- I don't know therewasa girl down the street that played piano, Dorothy Green, who played very good, she was a very talented little girl. And she read and did very well, she used to play in the school and everything, so a couple of years later, I think I was junior in high school, she'd run over to a town called Jacksonville, to take some advanced lessons. There was a school over there --
Yeah?
Illinois University or something like that. Illinois Western or something --
Yeah.

And when she was over there she stopped by a music store, Johnson's -- J. Bart Johnson, and J. Bart Johnson was a band director and he had a son that played drums and a little xylophone, so she talked to him if he'd give a few lessons. So I went over, lot of times I'd go over and he'd be playing a job the night before and I'd have to take -- get up at 4:00 in the morning to go over.
Why did it take so long?

The train is only time I could get it. See I'd try to -- I'd take a 6:00 o'clock train and - get there at 7:00, the store had been open, so his wife would open the store so he wouldn't -- they'd open it, but nobody would be in for business --
No.
-- unless his brother would open it.
So they also sold records --
Oh.
-- so they'd let -- I'd say can I hear this? Sure, they'd go and get records --
Yeah.
-- so I'd hear -- that's why --
Yeah.
-- that's why I got interested in hearing things --
Yeah.

-- and so sometimes he'd be playing a job and he would sleep late and wouldn't show up and instead of going back at noon, there was a 4:00 o'clock -- there was a 3:30 train back, I wouldn't get back till 5:00 o'clock, so a lot of times I go there and stay all the day and that and he wouldn't see me.
Oh.
But they let me go up he wasn't coming and they had up in the second floor they had a xylophone up there and it was a good one --
Yeah.
-- and so I could play on that one a little bit, you know it was fun.
Yeah. Yeah.

And then he tried to help, he played enough he could read and take --play parts. He was trying to show me what he could. He said, 'I'm really not a xylophone player. He said that's just a sideline with me because I'm a drummer.' MS VANCE: Yeah.
He said, 'But if I can help you, I will.' But I paid him. And I took a few lessons from him and then
I'd go over so many times and nothing would happen --
Yeah.
-- I just got --
Discouraged, get up at 4:00 in the morning.
And I'm wasting a day when I could --
Yeah.

So then, in my last year in high school this Dorothy Green down the street and another girl were going to Chicago to try out for Chataqua, which was a tent thing, and it happened in all the small towns in the Midwest in those days, I don't know if you ever heard about it. It was like Lyceum and like I seen them in Chataqua, in the wintertime it was Lyceum, Beards-town and they'd have -- they'd come into, say, Georgetown, they'd put up a tent in one of the school yards.
Yeah?
And they'd have lectures, they'd have oh, different musical things. Oh, maybe a string quartet one afternoon, and something else --
Well they --
-- and they have tickets you buy by the Chamber of Commerce, and everybody in town would go they'd by a weekly ticket.
I see.
For afternoon or nights.
Yeah.

They'd have a program layed and out. So this is the sort of thing -- the one girl had been in Chataqua before. So, they inveigled me to go up with them. So -- well I can't read, I thought what am I gonna -- so they said, you play. And I was playing a few solos, back in high school, at that time in assemblies --
Yeah.
Dorthy would play for me.
YEAH.

So they said come on up, why not. So my mother said, what have you got to lose, you're going to the University of Illinois in the Fall, mean, go on up, you can travel for nothing. I used to travel on the railroad cause my father was a railroader, for nothing.
I see, so the people that were in it, were they employed in it?
No, no. She was still in high -- my gade in high school. She was just going up with this other girl who was a concert violinist -- see?
Well --
And Lived in the town.
Oh, I see.
See what I mean?
Yes.
So they took me along as a -- like a novelty thing, see?
Well, I never.
And I played a couple of solos --
Yeah, yeah.
I don't remember what it was, I don't remember what they were now.
Yeah.
I think that's about four or five things is all I knew.
Yeah. Could you read music then?
No, I couldn't read music. I knew what the notes were --
Yeah, but you couldn't --
When you say read, I mean I knew the notes --
Yeah.
-- I knew the keys and all that sort of thing --
Sure.
But I mean to -- to be a fast reader, like you'd have to to be a professional --
Yeah.
-- so I went up and we -- everyday we had two or three auditions, we'd just take them --I had two
cases and I'd go in with them and sit with them and set up and here we'd go. So we were in the Fine Arts Building in Chicago and --
Uh -- you went to Chicago?
Yeah, we went up to Chat -- that's where we did our auditions.
Oh.

And it was in the Spring, I think around April. Or May, around the first of May. And we'd do an audition for the people in the Fine Arts Building. Ah, it was -- wait a minute, what was the name of that girl. Anyway the guy's name was Jack Tebo who came to me, I remember his name, and he said, (unintelligible) going off in the summer, Chattanooga; the fellow had to be operated on. We need somebody and I can't find anybody. He said, 'You'll be perfect.' I said, 'But I can't read, I don't know' -- He said, 'You'll learn the thing, they all played, it'll be simple for you.' I said, 'No. I can't.' I was scared to death. I didn't even know how to talk to him.
Weren't you kind of thrilled though?
No, I wasn't thrilled at all. Actually, I wasn't thrilled at all.
You were frightened?
Yes, I knew -- the idea was thrilling --
Yeah.
To think that I -- the idea to do it, but
Yeah.
-- I wasn't -- wasn't --
Yeah, capable.

No. I wasn't capable. So he kept wiring me to come. That he wanted me there. So I was graduating from high school. In May. So my mother said to me, "Look. It's still the same thing; in September you're going to go to Champaign, go to the University of Illinois. So what have you got to lose, all he can do is send you home? You can travel for nothing to Chicago. And she said if you make it, you might enjoy it. In the summer.
Yeah, yeah.
And so I was a little scared, but finally I thought, well, if he's insistent -- if he's willing to take a chance, I am too.
It's not your fault, then.
So she's right, all they can do is send me home.
Well.
So I went up and we had a week of rehearsals, and I caught onto it and we were all playing different parts. And I suddenly realized that I could fit in, I knew I could do it.
Yeah.
I knew that it would take time, but I knew I could do it and the lead man, by the name of Forest Hardy, was a drummer and a xylophone player -- he was very encouraging.
Oh.

He said, 'You got great hands. You got great hands, it'll be no problem for you.' I said, 'What do you mean?' He said, 'Well I don't know you don't play it like a drummer or anything.' He said, 'You got good hands on it.' He said, 'In another week you'll have it all down.'
Well, explain one thing to me. What were the instruments, how many were there?
Everybody played -- they had three or four of them across the stage. Besides the others --
Oh.
-- they'd double. Like a trumpet player played trumpet and he played the marimba xylophone.
Oh, I see.
And saxophone player he played em -- bass player played them, the drummer played, and then all of us would go up, but I was just the steady one, see?
Yeah.
It was good.
How old were they?
Oh, they were older than I was.
Yeah.
I think I was 17.
And they were in their 20's, or something?
Oh, yeah. One of them, Forrest of course, was married -- he was 20, something.
And they were a professional group that was being paid?
Oh, yeah. Yeah. So I got paid, too, you know, I mean it was a job, which I was very happy about.
Well what -- what was the job exactly? Where did you play? Where and back?
All over the Midwest. We played Peru, Indiana. We played Lincoln, Illinois --
AAfternoon concerts?
-- we played all these little towns --
Yeah, with the afternoon and evening concerts --
Yeah, the tents would be set up --
I see.
-- they'd move the tent every week from a different town --
I get it -- I get it yeah.
And you'd just keep going around, do you follow?
Yes, I do follow, sure.
Just like a circus.
Yeah, sure. So -

So, in the FALL, after that tour was over, I went to Champagne. And I really enjoyed it. I went home for a couple of days and then went over to the University of Illinois and registered, started. Well, in November I get a call from this same Jack Techo, who's producing an act called The Collegians, who were going in vaudeville, they were going to California. This was 1925. I couldn't stand it. I just -- I left school --
Well when -- Red --
-- went back to Chicago --
Red, listen. Tell me something, what were you going to study at college?
I don't know, I guess I was gonna -- you mean what --
Yeah, what were you supposed to be going to do, what did you think you were going to do with your life?
I don't know. I was just going for a BA. degree, my brothers and sisters were all college --
Well did --
They studied engineering.
-- they go for engineering?
What? They studied engineering. One brother was a geologist and the other was a geologist.
Oh.
They were all into mining.
Yeah. So you were going to do something the same?
Well I started that because I wanted to -- I wasn't quite decided what I wanted to do.
Yeah. But up until then, it never occurred to you do anything but go to college, huh?
That's all.
You just thought you would go to college and see what you were going to do.

I was interested in mining, because I -- and when I was 10 or so, my brother's job was for Texas Company down in Oklahoma and I used to go out and he was there when they opened the Osage Territory there. Indian Territory when they first came in --
OH.
So I used to travel all over in the daytime I'd go out with him. And it was interesting, all -- all the geologists, they'd meet in one of these farmhouses where they have the homecooking --
Yeah.
and it'd be out -- oh my goodness in the wilderness someplace, you see. It was a fascinating life.
Yeah, yeah.
And they'd have the table loaded and all
these geologists come in and they'd eat, my goodness, it was great. So I had a taste of it.
Yeah.
Then my other brother at that time was down in a coalmine out in a little town in New Mexico. So I'd go out there some summer, maybe split it.
Your family was nice and close. You -- everybody was close with each other, I mean -- it was nice to go to your brother's wasn't it --
It --
I mean there was close affection, bonds?
I think so, yeah. Oh, apparently except that --
Cause they had the kid brother come?
Except that the one in Oklahoma, never gave -- never -- never liked the idea of me becoming a musician. You know. Oh, they were so against it.
Was that the oldest brother?
No, that was the second brother.
Oh, he didn't like it, huh?
No, he didn't.
Didn't think it was good enough for you, huh? Good enough career?
Well no. He came to Chicago, I remember, at the end of that Chataqua thing. I know my mother had told

him and he and his wife came up, they came to see my mother, and father, and he said something about, 'You're not going to keep doing this.' I said, 'No.' I said, 'I don't know, I haven't even thought about it,' I said. -- He said, 'No, don't get thinking this way at all.' He said, 'Musicians, they're all drunkards or dope fiends and things like this. You can't -- you can't go this way at all.'
In those days they said musicians were dope fiends?
That's what he thought?
Did they?
Yeah, that's what he -- that's his opinion.
Was that right?
And he had a very low opinion of musicians. And I think he always did.
You never cured --
Yeah, he never -- he never recognized -- I changed my name, you know?
And you mean you didn't stay in touch?
No, we never stayed in touch, I never stayed in touch with him after that.
Oh.
I never saw him for years.
Oh, really. But you did stay in touch with the other brother?
I went to school that Fall and I left.
Yeah.
And he was disgruntled with that, too.
Oh, that -- it's funny that it would be the second oldest and not the oldest. The oldest was all right, huh?
Well, the oldest was -- yeah, the oldest was a couple of years later he was in Phoenix and I came through with Oliver Shaw, I played Phoenix, it was a real small town, he was living there.
Phoenix was a small town?

Yeah. He had-- he was married and had two boys. And played this theater and he was the proudest thing in the world. That was the first inclination information that I had that he was -- it was good and --
Oh, that's good.
-- his oldest boy walked out on the stage and he knew -- he knew me from going to -- (unintelligible) was right out of Santa Fe.
Yeah.

I loved New Mexico when I was a kid. I used to run around all those mountains in those days and we used to go back in the hill country. They desert those towns where the 49 -- gold rush, you know they'd just leave -- left them.
Oh.
And the roads were overgrown, but this boy that I knew and we'd take.22's and we'd hike up to these places and they even had stoves with utensils on them and things like that.
How extraordinary.
And the churches and the -- of course the roof would be there, they're adobe, but they caved in and the --
Well you mean they'd heard that there was gold somewhere else and they just left --
No, when California they just left. There was mining, oh, probably silver mines, or zinc mines or something up there.
For heaven's sake.
And when they heard about the --
The gold --
-- the gold in California, they just up and left.
Yeah.
That was all through that country was like that.
How extraordinary.
But, -- [Recording Interruption]
Red -- well Red, let's see, I had to
interrupt us, but you were talking about the townsthere, in New Mexico --
Yeah, Madrid --
-- when you used to see your brother --
-- they called it Madrid, like Madrid in Spain, but it's Madrid there.
Oh, is it?
Yeah.
I see, I didn't know --
That's a ghost town now. I went there a couple of years ago and it's a ghost town.
Is it? Really?
Yeah, that's a beautiful little place.
Is it. Fancy that.
Ah -- anyway, when I played Phoenix, he was -- first inclination that I had that he -- and all through the time after that he was --
He supported --
Yeah, he used to write me if he heard something or if you did this or the other thing -- he heard -- he was very concerned with it.
Did he still play some piano?
Yeah, he played piano.
Did he ever accompany you at all?
No, no, no. He'd left home when I started
But you didn't go to the house and he had a piano --
He had a piano, but --
No, but I mean at his house?
No, after he went to college he never played too much.
Oh. Ah did -- where did your mother first hear you perform?
I don't know. I think -- I don't remember I think --
Where was it?

-- oh, I know what. I know. That last year I was in school, they was playing in the Princess Theater in Beardstown -- they had amateur contest. In the theater and there was a wonderful pianist in the pit by the name of Leo Boylen, who was a -- really a great -- he'd been with bands around territory bands --
Yeah, yeah.
-- and he played the silent pictures, he had all the gear, with the drums and everything, and he was a gas, I used to love to hear him play comedies and chases and things --
Yeah.
and so he played for me and I won, and

that's the first time she heard me play, I don't remember what I played right at the moment, I only had about four or five things I could play at that time, that I knew. I kept trying to play better all the time --
Yeah, yeah.
That's the first time and I won first prize, I remember that.
What did you-- was there anything involved with the first prize, that you --
I don't know just something --
Just something, yeah.
-- any prize or anything.
But I mean when you -- when you went professionally. When this -- when this Jack Tiboo, is that his name?
Jack Tiboo.
After you --

I think she came someplace during the summer. I think that my mother and sister came, I think it was Lincoln, Illinois, that's how I happen to remember that town, I think they came to Lincoln and heard us.
Yeah.
And --
They were kind of proud --
Yeah, they thought it was like fun.
Yeah.
They looked at it that was, as fun. And --
Well what had your father to say about this?
Well he didn't hear me, then.
Well what did he think about the fact you left college?
He never thought much about it, then he became ill. After that, and he had a stroke and he was ill after that for a number of years.
How old was he when he had a stroke?
How old was he?
Yes.
Gee, I don't remember now.
I mean, but he was in his middle years, huh? Or did he die youngish?
No, he was 50's -- he was close to 60 --
Oh, he was.
Up there. I guess he was in his 50's.
I really don't remember.
Yeah, so he never heard you?
I really don't remember. No, he never really heard me. He'd heard me around the house, which he didn't like, he didn't feel -- when he was sick he didn't like it.
Oh, no. Yeah.
And these -- used to get on his nerves.
Yeah.
I'd pound on that thing all the time, I realize that.
Well practicing gets on anybody's nerves.
Yeah, I know that. I realize that.
Yeah, well -- well all right, let's go back to -- so you left college and you joined this group. Well what was the group?
Collegians, I think was the name of it.
Oh yeah.

I have pictures and I met -- funny I met the trumpet player up at the festival up at Ojai in California the trumpet player came by and showed me a picture. He said he'd been a newspaperman in California and he retired in Ojai there, Ojai festival there -- jazz festival. And, I was shocked, I forget his name, I think it was -- forgot what his name was now. He showed me a picture and I think his name was Wentworth, or something like that -- no that wasn't it -- we had a nickname for him --
Yeah.

-- I don't know what it was. He used to, I remember we were out West on that trip and he used to go with no hat, up in the Northwest, it was freezing and I could remember saying, why don't you wear a hat. He was on a
Well, were they --
What?
Were they a group that had been working together, the Collegians?
Yeah, no it was a new idea, new group.
Oh, I see.
And it was about seven pieces. I got a picture of it someplace, but it was a piano, I forget -- it was a piano, trumpet, drums, saxophone --
Yeah, I see and they were playing jazz?
Yeah.
Well, when did you -- when did you first start playing syncopation?
Oh, from the very beginning --
You did?
-- I knew what that was. I knew that before I started playing. I was interested in that, cause a fella that worked with my father was a great piano player, I mean jazz piano player.
Really?
Yeah, he even had a music store in town and I used to go by and he used to play oh, play blues and all these ragtime pieces and --
Oh, no kidding?
And the piano player in the theater used to play wonderful ragtime playing, just improvising ragtime.
Was the piano player you were talking about --
Yeah, Leo Boylen, yeah he was wonderful at that, improvising, --
Is that right?
-- cause he'd improvise all those things for the cartoon comedies --
Oh yeah.
-- he was very adept at it. And I used to ask him how he does it, you know?
Yeah.
-- he just say, well I don't know I just -- just --
Yeah, yeah.
He had wonderful hands, and then this piano player used to play slow things, like slow blues and thing, just improvising.
Oh.

Just improvising. And then the river boats, you see, I heard -- I grew up listening to all the bands on the riverboats, like I first heard Bix Beiderbecke and Frankie Trumbauer and Ray Ludwig and all these fellas out of St. Louis, cause at that time, in well -- say 1908, by 1918, around
there, St. Louis was really the hub of jazz, more than people really give credit for.
Yeah.
That's where Louis was. I heard Louis on the boats. In those early years --
Did you, really?
-- in the '20's, too, because see the excursion boats would come out of St. Louis. They'd go up and down the Mississippi and the Illinois and all these rivers.
Yeah.
And during the summertime in my hometown that was a big thing. They didn't have a dance hall here --
Yeah.
-- all the dancing was done on the excursion boats.
Yeah, I see.

Say a department store, like Kleins Department Store, if you traded there they'd have an all-day excursion, go down the locks, down to the Meredosia and you'd get on 8:00 in the morning and in the afternoon the band would play, --
Well when did the band come off, same time as you did? I mean would they go --
No, they lived -- they lived on the boat.
Oh, they lived --
Yeah, they lived, that was a job. They lived on the boat.
Oh.
They stayed on that boat. They were hired for the summer --
Oh, I see.
-- or for that time. The job was there. They had -- cabins --
Oh, they did?
-- just like the Captain, and the crew.
Is that right?

And the piano player would go up and play the calliope. When the boat would dock, like if it was a moonlight excursion -- say it left at 8:00 o'clock, well at 7:30, you -- all over the town you'd hear that calliope --
I see.
-- and then he would be playing tunes up on the calliope. That was the signal, sure.
Were these all black guys, usually? Oh, no, because you said Bix and --
What do you mean black guys?
Well, I mean were they black musicians --
No, they were white musicians.
When you said Louis and --
Some were -- some boats were -- some were/
Yeah, I see.
They were different. Different boats, different, yeah.
Yeah.
Most of the stevedores that worked on the boats were black.
Yeah.
And we had packet boats and all that -- packet boats, well it was like shipping lines. They still have them on the river. They still have big packet boats, coal boats.
Well, what does that mean, packet boats? What does it --
Just what it says? Packet, ship package, ship -- hogs --
Really?
-- furniture, everything --
Really?
-- on a boat and they would be unloaded by black --
Yeah.
-- stevedores.
Well they didn't have any music?
No, not the packets. No, no, they were strictly ah --
Freight?
Freight, yeah, sure.
Water freight. Yeah.
But the excursion boats were also boat lines, they had schedules laid out for maybe a month ahead.
Yeah. Well the reason I asked you about the black musicians, is cause you know you always here about Fate Marable and all the different guys.
Well he worked on a boat --
On the River boats.
He worked --
Well I didn't realize that Bix and Frankie Trumbauer played those boats?
Oh, yes, that's where they started in St. Louis.
Oh, so that -- just as jobs.

YEAH. I later roomed with Frankie in Paul Whiteman's band -- talk about -- and I was a kid when I stood there and listened to him, he was my idol. My goodness I used to think he was the greatest thing since hash. Frankie Trumbauer. And Bix, I thought, oh, my. And, he was.
Well I mean who -- I mean would they be a part of a group --
They were a set band. They were hired on that boat. They --
Well who else was in that? Band? Can
you remember? Well drummer was Ray Ludwig, I don't remember, now. My goodness, you're talking about --
I know I am --
-- 60 years ago.
I know it -- I know it.
Nearly. I don't remember that.
It'd be like five or six -- five or six musicians?
Yeah, there'd be a trumpet, trombone or saxophone, and three rhythm. Be six --
Yeah.
-- at least, maybe seven sometimes.
How about that?
And sometimes they were bigger. Fate Marable worked -- I heard him on a boat.
Yeah.
I heard Louis on the Capitol.
Oh.

I forget the boat was, I think, that Frankie was on. Ah, don't remember. I know one of the boats was the Julie Belle Swain, which number of years later I saw down in New Orleans, but when I opened the Royal Sonesta, about six-seven years ago.
Really?

Yeah. And, fella said, 'Come down and I'll take you around the city, and I said, 'What boat?' he said, 'Julie Belle Swain,' I nearly fell down. Because later this Mel Hewlitt and the Skinner boys worked on that same boat.
Really?
Yeah. And, oh, the boats were -- the River was a beautiful thing in those days.
Yeah, I bet it was.
They hadn't cut through to the Chicago River, which made a passage from Chicago down to St. Louis, see you can go all the way, the Great Lakes, yeah, down to New Orleans.
Yeah -- well -
But the hub there was St. Louis, they had other great bands, like Gene Roderick, was the biggest band and record companies.
Really?
And he played in the theater in St. Louis. This was a wonderful band. Great musicians.
Oh.
There was more jazz in St. Louis than there was in Chicago or --
And what was that, like 1920?
Oh, before that.
Before that? Ah --
I think I was oh, I don't I know -- I don't know exactly, years, I can't --
Yeah --
I can't place years --
No.
In that respect -- every year I used to be on that boat all the time.
Oh, you did?
Oh, yeah, excursion boats, everybody made that.
Yeah.
I used to go on mainly -- course guys to dance that had dates they'd go on the bands --
Yeah.
-- beautiful summer nights on the river it's nice --
Yeah.
-- and cool, too.
Yeah.
-- But I'd go on just to listen to the music --
Yeah.
-- and --
You would just hang out right there --
Oh yeah, hang out see the band and every-
thing. They'd be playing jazz things and I loved it, I just loved to listen to it.
Yeah.
So, from the very beginning, and in the beginning in those days before I ever had a job I was trying to play jazz, I was --
Yeah.
Ah --
Yeah, well you were really very lucky to be exposed to talent like Bix and Frankie Trumbauer, so early when youwere hardly even playing --
I don't think if I ever played, I'd still be a jazz fan today.
Yeah.
In other words, if I wasn't a musician today --
Yeah.
-- I'd probably be the most ardent jazz fan there is.
Yeah. Yeah.
Because I really enjoyed it and then after -- I always had a feel -- I always had a yen I wanted to play.
Yeah.
I always had that feeling, but I -- I
don't know just from never -- I didn't feel I had anything --
Yeah.
I didn't -- I just -- it was like I -- a hobby with me more --
Yeah.
-- I never thought of -- about being a musician as such.
Yeah, you --
Never thought about it.
No.
-- and yet, it just developed. One thing led to another.
Yeah.
And I never took life very serious in those days, anyway. I never got all filled up with ambition like my brothers were.
You were easy going?
Yes, right from the beginning, I guess, I was that way. I think I was. I think they thought I was too much that way.
Did they?

But I -- I really had a wonderful mother. She -- when my older brother used to rant and rave about me being a musician and all, she'd say, 'Well you gotta do what you gotta do. That's what you want to do, you do it.'
Yeah.
You don't have to --
She was very understanding?
Oh, yeah. She was at us -- tried to get us out of that small town. She said, you've got to get out of here.
Oh, she did?
Oh, yeah. You can't -- you'll never -- you'll never be happy, you'll deteriorate in a small town like --
And yet that meant she was going to lose you in a sense, all of you. If you all left?
Yeah, we all did.
Well --
My brothers left high school and went right to college. They never came back to live there --
They never came back?
-- they came back to visit -- and she'd go and visit them --
Yeah. What about Portia, did she leave?
Well she came back and taught school there for awhile, but after my --
Yeah.
-- father died and they sold my -- we also owned a house downtown in Beardstown, down on the Square --
Yeah?
And which when we had the other place, where I grew up, we rented to a doctor --
Yeah?
-- and so my father died, we finally got her -- my sister got her to sell the big place, it was too much --
Yeah?
-- and so the doctor we got him to leave and he went to someplace, another building and so they went there at that time and she enjoyed it there --
Yeah.
-- she had a lot of friends and they would come by downtown.
Yeah.
But she'd come and visit, she could travel -- she had a pass and she could travel anyplace in the country.
Even after your father died?
Oh, yes. Oh, she had a lifetime pass.
Really? Isn't that great, I think that is absolutely marvelous that the railroad did that.
She used to come to the coast to visit me whenI moved to California.
Even after your fatherdied she was able to --
Oh, she had a lifetime pass. Oh, yeah.
That's wonderful, isn't it?
Rest of her life.
And as long as your father was alive, you could travel for free?
That's right, as long as he was working --
Any member of his family?
No, no. As long as I was dependent.
Ah --
You see?
Yeah, I see.
LIke my older brothers when they started working and got their own families they -- no, no.
No. Well then your father must've made fairly good money then, Red, for all the boys to go to college, everybody to go to college?
Well I guess for those years, I don't -- exactly -- I know that she got a pension when he died.
She did?
Yeah. I know she had a pension.

Well I mean but was it -- did she have a -- I mean, well you know, today, if everybody was going to go to college, everybody is going to go crazy trying to pay for it. I know it wasn't the same thing then, but even so it was it ate into what you had. So, I mean did you --

Well my father didn't -- wasn't too anxious about them going, now he didn't see college like my mother did, I'm afraid. And, in fact, she would say -- save money to help Glenn -- way before Howard Glenn -- Wayne went before Howard did.
Oh, the second --
The second one went to college before the oldest one did. He went the first year, and then Howard went the next year --
Yeah.
-- so they were both in college, but she was helping, she -- and she was going to work -- he was going to work, he said, I'm going if I have to work. He said I'm going if I have to work.
Yeah.
And my father wanted him to get a job for a couple of years, and decide but he was -- he knew exactly what he wanted to be, what he wanted to do --
Yeah, I mean -- and that's fairly unusual.

And they both did. Both were all interested in it. But Howard when he got through, he worked for a year, and then in the summers they used to go out to Great Falls, Montana, and work. And work in the coal mines -- I mean work in the zinc mines --
Yeah.
Anaconda Copper Company.
Yeah, and make enough money to help with the following year.
So they really were ambitious about going to college --
Yeah.
That's --
Well, listen where were you when your father died, what stage were you at?
I was in Chicago.
Working with who?
Oh, I don't remember, I don't remember at the time.
Vic Young?
I think I was in vaudeville someplace --
Yeah, and did you go home?
Yeah, sure. Oh, yeah My brothers came we all --
Yeah.
-- we all came home. And we buried him up in a little town that I went to see the grave last year, in Roseville, Illinois, my mother and father are buried there.
Oh.
And my mother died on the coast and we had a service out there, and then my brother, Glenn, was shipped -- we shipped her to Roseville and were buried here by my father.
Oh.
In Roseville.
That was nice.
So, last year when I was playing in Chicago, I rented a car and drove over, stayed all night, near Monmouth, Illinois.
Yeah.
And it was a lovely little town, that's where they were raised and my uncles were all farmers around there --
Oh.
My mother's family was there too.
Yeah.
It's a little town, it's nice.
Yeah, nice -- nice that they both --
So I drove over and my brother buried them the and I saw their graves a---
Well, that was nice.
Yeah.
Well, listen, now I'm getting you off the track, let's go back to the Collegiates.
To where?
The Collegians. When you joined them.
OH, Collegians. We made a trip to the West Coast, we started and we went up through the northwest,

played towns like oh, Montana, Great Falls, there was gambling there, I remember we played a theater and I was intrigued, I was so young, it was the first time I had ever seen gambling. Like that. And,
Well what --
-- right off the street, just like it is in Vegas now. That's the way it was -- you see gambling in those years was prevalent out West.
Oh.
And they --
It wasn't against the law?
Well they voted -- oh, it's been gone for years, they voted it out in Montana, I think, in the -- in the early '30's, or late '20's, --
Oh, Oh.
In that state. But then we went out to Seattle --
Well what were they gambling, roulette -- and --
Everything, just like Vegas. 21, roulette, dice --
I SEE. Yeah.
Yeah. Right off the street.
Yeah. Did you gamble.
No, I don't gamble --
You don't?
I play the slot machines probably a little bit... and go
Yeah. Yeah. So you went out to the West Coast --
Went out to the West Coast, we played Seattle, and we played down the Coast, down to Los Angeles. And then I got sick in Los Angeles, I got typhoid fever.
Really?
So they had to leave me there.
And you were what, about 19?
In Los Angeles, yeah.
And you got typhoid?

Yeah, I got it on my way down. So I was sick -- I was very sick. And I remember I stayed at a little hotel, San Carlos, or something or other, across from the Biltmore. So, the booking agents of the Orpheum time looked after me and they came every day and they got doctors and they took care of me.
Honestly? (unintelligible)?
Yeah.
That was pretty good. I don't know that a booking agent would do that today, to -- do you?
Huh?
I don't know that a booking agent would

do that today, to a member of a group, do you think they would? Well, I think they left liked me and yes, they had to. And this Jack Tiboo in Chicago, made the calls, and with the connection in Chicago ---
Is that right?
-- they looked out. I couldn't be moved.
No.
And, oh gosh, I was sick. And then --
That's not funny typh -- now typhoid's back for hearing too.
I know that. I lost my hair, it came out and everything.
Really.
When I came back in it was thin, yeah. I was really sick.
You were quite critically sick.
Yes.
Hm.

It's the first time I had ever been sick. I didn't know what being sick was like before. I came through it all right. But the interesting thing about being sick that year, was that now, let's see it was '26, then. 1926. And I walked over in the park, which is in Los Angeles, that park. I forget the name of it, it's right downtown. I used to sit in the sun. And I could walk -- just make it across the street.
I was weak, see?
Yeah.

I was getting strength back and finally one day I walked around the park, after a few days I got so I could walk pretty well. So one day I walked out of the park on the other side and I walked down and here was Rube Wolfe working in a [transho De- Marco] Theater.
