And I'd be on trains and I'd study the harmony books, all these sorts of things. That's when I did it on the trains. Now the practical side of reading music I think that's quite -- people think that's hard.
It's a question of a habit --
It's like learning to read words--
Habit isn't it.
Yeah, just practice.
Yeah, practice.
And confidence.
Yeah.
All it is is confidence.
Yeah.
Cause if you know -- if you go in a studio and you see a part and a red light comes on, if you know you're going to play it, you play it.
Yeah.
But if for one second, you think, maybe I wonder if I'm going to miss it, you'll miss it.
Yeah.
It's just psychological or something.
Yes.
That -- know that you can (unintelligible) that music --
Yes, and there you go, yeah.
Cause I think I learned better to read, after Whiteman's band, for Frankie influenced me very much, Frankie Trumbauer, in reading.
Yeah. Well, he was so fast for those days...
First time I heard him on the boats he didn't read.
He didn't?
No, he didn't read.
I didn't know that.
He didn't read. Most of those guys, I think Bix read, but the rest of them -- I think maybe the piano player and Bix and that early days -- I don't remember the names (unintelligible)
of all of them --
Yeah.
When I was rooming with Frankie, later, couple of times, I asked him, 'How'd you start to read?' cause he read fantastic then, and he had a tremendous technique.
Yeah.
He had it all --
Yeah.

He said, I realized that I had to learn how to read, so I bought every book, every piece of music I could get. And he said, I started out, the first four months, every day, locked myself in the house and I just started to read, and he said, I never read it twice, if I made a mistake I didn't stop, I just kept reading. All day long, much as I could go -- I'd get tired go get something to eat and go back and do it.
Yeah.
And he said, 'That's just the way --'
Yeah.
And he read as well as anybody I ne -- ever knew.
Yeah.
He could read anything.
And then he had all that facility in his fingers --
Yeah, but he never played that way, people used to say, My God, all that technique and everything and yet of course, you must realize, they used to ask me about Bix, about Bix playing.
Yeah.
And they said, "If they were alive now, how would they play?"
Yeah.
I said, "Well, I don't really know," I know that they were -- that Frank was a great musician --
Yeah.
And in the style, of those days was to play pretty.
Yeah.
It was to play melodic, not --
Yeah.
-- you didn't show technique --
You didn't have to dance fireworks?
No, you didn't say, oh boy here is the way it is --
Yeh, it was music.
-- do a technical thing just for technical sake, to show that --
That's right, that's right --
-- you're a jazz technique man.
That's right.

Or used it to the extent of bravado, no. He'd turn right -- Yet, I've seen him play solos and nice solos, Whiteman band, and then turn around and go and triple tongue it -- tremendous technique, fast, just for laughs for the guys or something. That's -- Then sit down. He a couple of people a couple of things.
You should come back and tell the --
He was one of my favorite people. He was my favorite --
What was he like, was he witty?
Wonderful sense of humor. I don't know he says -- very accomplished, he was unlike Bix, he never drank that much --
Yeah.
He'd fly, he'd fly an airplane. He taught Jack Tea -- I mean Charlie Teagarden how to fly.
Really?
Oh, he was a pilot in the early '20's.
In those days?
OH, yes.
Isn't that strange.
And he had a wonderful. He used to make my slap hammers.
He did?
He made my slap hammer, when I was with
Whiteman -- I used to break them. And he used to -- he used to make, them sew between shows, he'd have a needle and thread and those buckskin things, and fix them.
For heaven's sake.

So, finally one day he said to me, I'm going to make you a pair you won't break. I said, 'Great, that'd sure be great,' because I'd take the [Symphony six] to make them, and he'd sew them and everything. So he got two steel golf shafts or rods, whatever they were, and he cut them -- had them cut off, and he had washers welded on them. He must've spent a week wrapping this with yarn and put felt on it, and finally put the buckskin outside. So he handed them to me on the first show. We did, I think when we were in Cleveland, or someplace, and I think we were doing four or five shows -- I forget what it was -- and I played the first show and they were wonderful. Second show they were wonderful. Third show, I thought oh, this is going to be the greatest, I'm so happy. The fourth show, the thing -- things started to happen, see. Fourth show things started to happen.

At the fifth show that day, the washers had cut through all -- the whole thing and I'm gouging wood out of this rivet. This thing -- sparks are flying off the thing and everytime I hit it, there'd be a gouge with this tremendous thing, and I had to keep hitting I was doing the act, and Whiteman's standing there. So I had to keep going, I must've ruined a dozen
bars, I had to send away and order the bars, and he's sitting there, laughing like, I finally made them --
Did he not realize what was happening, but
Yeah, but he was there, he was laughing about it. Next day he had a couple of new pair, he knew they were wrong.
Oh, how funny, isn't that funny.
But he used to do funny little things, I was sitting on the stage and Ilooked at him, and my -- you know how people scratch their face like this?
Yeah.
Well it's hard to show you -- he sits there, he -- he'd be watching something. And be some act's Maybe that on, or -- I think at that time Red McKenzie was with us, --
Yeah.
-- so he's scratching his neck, so this is the way he did it. It's so silly scratchingup, he never scratched down. If he scratched his head, he'd go --
(LAUGHTER)
How funny. He was a real relaxed guy. He was an adorable man;
Yeah, he was just a wonderful man to be around. And I don't know --
Well listen, we're off again --
Yeah, I know, but I can't help it.
We'll come back to him again, because we've got time, we want to.
But you know, later so many guys -- well Benny Carter used to tell me, gosh Frank was really his idol --
Idol, I heard that.
And I'll tell you another one, ah -- ah guy's with Basie --
The flute --
Huh?
-- ah that guy that used to play tenor --
Lester Young.
Oh, Lester. Oh, really?
Lester told me that he -- we were talking --
Yeah.
-- you know in Kansas City, nat -- and Frankie lived in Kansas City --
Yeah.

-- in fact he died in Kansas City and -- and his wife still lives there in Kansas City. And he said that he used to try to imitate the sound of the C-melody saxophone, the sound that Frankie Trumbauer got on tenor.
Eh -- isn't that extraordinary.
You never heard that before?
Well it --
He seemed to say -- I've heard him say it
two or three times.
I had heard that --
But I think he knew that I knew Frankie.
Yeah. No, I had heard that -- and that actually I mean I think there's something, that's not hard to believe is it?
No. When you think of it--
When you -- it's not hard to believe.
If you go and play an old record of our time --
Yeah, something of Lester's?
Get the similar --
Yeah, there is something --
On most of those records, he played E-flat alto and C-melody --
Yeah.
-- both -- but those records of Bix and those early records were all an C-melody.
Oh, yeah.
They were all an C-melody, it's like --
Yeah.
Now you get the ones on C-melody and then get Lester's and you'll see the difference.
And there was that light -- that light.
Yeah, that light flow that he had --
That's right, flow, exactly.
That you got it --
Like the wind.
Yes. From a to -- a great technique being used wisely.
That's right.
Not exhibited.
That's right, just made use of.
Right.
As required.
As required, and the flow that was there. Not that pup-plup-plup. That.
Exactly.
Or thing that you get.
Right, right.
The flow -- the beautiful flow of it.

Well it's very interesting that -- that Lester would have heard it and -- and felt that -- and had that feeling for it then. Cause he was young then. I mean that was before -- wasn't it -- that was before Lester -- yeah.
Oh, well he -- Frank was playing my goodness back -- Frank and Bix were playing before the 1920's.
Yeah.
They were working -- they were working --
Yeah, yeah.
They were very young kids. Frank was just a talented guy that couldn't read --
Yeah.
But that had great ears -- had --
Yeah.
-- and could play. But good facility.
How did they come together?
In St. Louis.
Yeah.
I don't know they just drifted together.
Because -- Well were they good friends?
Yeah, they were friends.
Yeah.
They were friends. They enjoyed playing with one another.
Yeah, you mean they were better friends, performing --
Yeah.
-- or playing? Than maybe off the stand --
Yeah.
-- I mean because Bix --
Well Frank was more outgoing.
Yeah.
And he was a doer.
YEAH.
More than Bix, I would say.
Yeah.
Bix was kind of a -- what's the word, I don't want to say it wrongly. But he was very timid --
A dreamer?
No, kind of a timid guy, you know, he was kind of milk-toasty in other words, --
Was he really?
-- he wasn't a -- he wasn't --
He wasn't --
-- a pusher in any way.
No, wasn't aggressive.
He was very polite, oh, wonderful manners --
Gentle?

Yeah, cause I can remember one time going with Mildred when he and Harry Barris were living together and the gin bottles were all over the joint, but he like -- oh man he got up, offered Mildred the chair, Oh, Mildred, happy to -- you know, but polite to the end.
Yeah.
Shame isn't it, huh?
It is a shame.
Yeah.
But --
He just started --
Now, Frank in the daytime would be out doing things.
Yeah, wasn't Frank -- was Frank any older than Bix, a year or two older?
I don't know that.
NO.
When you're that age, you don't think about two or three years older --
NO, NO. NO.
You don't think that.
No, I just wondered if Bix was younger and -- thanks Red, and you know started drinking like young kids do sometimes, you know before they know enough to not.
Well I think in those years, I know we used to say, guys would come to New York when Bix was here and said 'Oh, I had a drink with Bix,' I think he was sort of a very kind guy that could not say no.
Yeah.
When somebody wanted to buy him a drink. He felt like--
Yeah, sure.
-- friendly --
Yeah.
-- and all this sort of thing.
Yeah, it's a shame.
-- well I think Frank was friendly, too, but in a different sort of way. I think that -- he was doing things, doing this or -- he was very mechanical --
Extraordinary, isn't it, huh?
Yeah.
Kind of amazing. Well listen, now where were we?
Well we can go on with a few stories about Frank if you want to.
Well, now, maybe we should.
All right, I'll go back when I was doing the single after I got out of -- after I met Victor Young and some of these people, that I worked around the, [Publix's] time in Chicago.
Well listen, I think Red what we should do is, there's just a little piece there that we ought to cover and move legitimately onto this place.
Well I was going to tie-in -- one thing, one person --
All right.
-- which will tie-in here.
Okay.
Cause I'd have to go back otherwise. Now I played in Madison, Wisconsin, at the Orpheum Theater, I was

doing a single now -- this was after I started with Paul Ash, and I had those records going in the dressing room and they were driving people nuts. I knew they -- I didn't realize -- as a kid you don't realize these things, cause you're -- you go to people's house and kids put on rock and roll and turn it up real loud --
Yeah.
-- you realize -- I suddenly realized maybe I was that way when I was young.
Yeah, yeah.
So the drummer in the pits said you sure like -- sure like that -- you know, that -- what-do-you- call it -- jazz music, don't you? That's what they called it then.
Playing hot.
Yeah, I was playing records; and Miff Mole, all these guys.
Ben Pollack or not that early?
Yeah, well any jazz player just about everything I could, as much as I could carry -- and when I'd get too much, I'd go back to Chicago and leave them and I was always buying them.
Yeah.
So the drummer for the pit came up and he said, 'Sometime I want you to go out, there's a fella playing out here in a roadhouse, plays real good blues.' I said, 'Oh, yeah?'
He said, I think you'd enjoy hearing him, cause you enjoy this music so much. I said, All right, I'd like to go. And he was the drummer and I hung out with drummers a lot --
Yeah.
-- and they'd maybe take me into restaurants in town and a lot of times, they'd be married and they'd invite me out to their house --
Yeah.
-- dinner and things --
Yeah.
-- I guess they thought I was a young kid they felt a little sorry for me.
Yeah.
So I quit the theater one night and we went out to this roadhouse. I heard this guy play, he just thrilled me. Played me so nice and so warm and everything --
What was -- piano?
Huh? Trumpet.
Oh.

So now we come to New York, Frankie Trumbauer says, 'I'm on a record date tomorrow, you're on it,' and he said, 'there's a new trumpet player in town.' Well I met this trumpet player in the -- in Madison, when I was there. And I got -- he came down to the theater a couple of times. Great -- very young. This is in the early '30's. So I go on the date

and I'm setting up and everything and in walks this kid. And Frank says, "Hey Red, I want you to meet somebody" and I turned around and he said, "I want you to meet Bunny Berigan." And Bunny said, "I know him." It was the trumpet player from Madison. Isn't that wild? Years later.
Years later? Honestly?
That was in the '20's. And I met him here I guess in 19 -- well I guess '31 or '2, so it's a very few years later, not too many years later.
Well I mean, Red --
He came right from Madison to New York.
Hold it a minute, just a second --
Well now wait a minute, well now before we do that, since we're talking about Bunny. I just have to say to you, I mean it's funny that you got that opportunity hearing Bunny all those years before --
Yeah, yeah.
-- when he was so young. What would have -- he have been, about 18?
Oh, my goodness I think --
Oh, not that, maybe even, huh?
Well I think I was 18 or 19. I'm not sure about my age at that time.
Yeah.
I mean --
But he was younger? Or was he about your age?
I don't remember --
Yeah.
In those years I never thought much about age, I suppose if I went back and looked it up --
Yeah.
-- I could probably gauge.

Well the only reason I'm asking you that when you said some years later and in the record session with Frankie, in New York, and I mean Bunny wasn't all that old even when he -- when he started off in New York, he wasn't all that old either, was he -- it seems to me, was he?
He was young -- see his father played trumpet too.
Oh, did he?

Oh, yeah, because he used to go by -- his father used to come to New York and I used to get together on the sessions, maybe for a month or two, when he'd get his lip -- you know, practice together -- play together.
Yeah, yeah. No, kidding.
That's what Bunny told me.
Yeah.
Well I -- he said, well I can't -- couple of times I wanted to do something, 'No,' he said, 'my father's
here and we're playing everyday."
Bunny -- when I first came to New York, you know, I went out -- the Goodman's got me a place right near them on Long Island then, well Jackson Heights, remember you were --
Oh, yeah.
-- in Forest Hills? And we was in Jackson Heights, and Bunny was around the corner, Bunny had a place around the corner, lived there too.
Oh, yeah.

But what I wanted to say to you, was since we're on that subject, we said we would talk about various musicians, but I mean I have to ask you if you don't feel, I mean, surely, there wasn't ever a white trumpet player that played more than Bunny, was there, to your way of thinking? Or do you think I'm wrong in saying that?
You mean in those days, you mean? Talking about --
Well --
-- I think Bunny was one of the great trumpet players.
I see.
I think he was warm --
He had a beautiful tone --
-- he had a great sound -- oh, a wonderful
glorious sand.
And he had a wonderful soul for you.
That's right, that's right, and he had a great jazz feel --
He had a terrific jazz feel.

I thought he had a wonderful feel. He was wonderful. That's why when I was making my first records, he was the first one I thought of, because -- you see there was nobody for me to be around, except people that played jazz.
Yeah.
You know when they say, well who did you -- who did you learn from or who did you do this --
Yeah.
-- nowadays they say who was your idol. And if they played tenor they'll pick out a tenor man.
Yeah.
And if they're a piano player they'll say it's Art Tatum, or Teddy Wilson or --
Yeah, yeah.
Somebody --
Yeah.
-- but there was nobody playing my instrument and jazz was just a melodic line --
Yeah.
And it didn't matter to me --
What you were playing, it's --
No, it didn't matter whether it was saxophone, trumpet or anything --
It was the music you were playing.
I realized that some instruments are more adapted -- technically --
Yeah.
Than everything --
Yeah.
So I started thinking of my own instrument in a technical way.
Yeah.
Of what it means. So -- I don't know, I know that early years I played more legato --
Yeah.
-- than I did later -- on.
Yeah.
-- I think, in those early days, and when I was on the staff at Chicago, and playing with Victor Young when he had the programs, I played more melodic. Than I did later, I don't know.
Yeah.
Course what --
Well maybe you were expec -- maybe it was more expected of you, too? Or required of you, was it?
Up to that time you heard xylophones on the radio, Lucky Strike dance orchestra. All this sort of thing. They all played fast --
OH, YES.
-- that's what they used, triple fast, an exhibition type thing --
Yeah, that's right classic.
-- with an accordion, like B. A. Roth Rolfe always had two or three xylophones players.
Yeah.
-- playing fast -- the thing.
Yeah.
And it was exciting for me as a xylophone player.
Yeah.
And I'd learned to do that.
Yeah.
I learnt to do that, too.
Yeah.
Because I felt that that was a means to get where maybe -- I wanted to be playing jazz.
Yeah, right. It was facet of your --
Yeah.
-- of your --
But Bunny, when I heard him in that road-

house, it affected me, it just was warm and harmony seemed to have that wonderful feel. When the guys would -- that would probably be a layman's way of saying, playing jazz -- he plays the blues, like he plays wonderful sounding things that --
Yeah.
-- that sound, and he did.
But he did have a real feel for blues, too.
Oh, yes.
He had that wonderful sound and feel for blues.
Oh, yeah.
And another thing --
Well, he sang
What he's saying so well -- I mean his horn?
YEAH, OH yeah.
Yeah.

And Red, another thing that impressed me very much about Bunny, was, you know, Bunny was - like I-- I used to hear, you know, when 52nd Street was going and so on and everybody was sitting in with everybody else, Bunny was the one guy that could go in and sit down where Jonah was and they were good friends, Jonah Jones, you know?
Oh, yeah.
And I mean he had -- it wasn't only that he had that much lip, I know his lip used to trick him
sometimes --
Yeah.
-- but he had a terrific lip and -- but it was -- he had that much fire, that he could compete with Jonah.
Oh, yeah.

And there weren't -- and I don't think I don't know that there have been other guys. I mean I don't mean to -- if I say, black, white -- I'm not saying it in any with racial overtones, or anything, I'm just saying that it's like everybody's heritage and everybody brings their own sort of thing. And I mean as a general rule there'd be perhaps more fire or something come out of a black trumpet player -
Oh, yeah.
-- and I mean- but Bunny was a guy that he -- he could compete and I -- and I mean guys like Jonah would accept that.
Well, I tell you, you know I don't really look at it as a thing of competing --
I don't mean it from the point of view of competition.
I'll tell you what -- I'll tell you what --
You know I didn't mean that.
Because I think when we say compete we overlook one of the most important factors of improvising and a most important part of jazz. When I say people -- I hear them
say, well they cut this or cut that --
Yeah.
Well I -- I cut them right out of my thinking --
Yes, I agree.
-- because here's the factor that I mean. Bunny could -- would come down and you say, sit in, with Jonah, all right. Most guys like Jonah and Bunny are affected, emotionally, by one another.
That's right.
And here is a lot of the secret of guys playing together. Now they weren't sitting there, with the idea that they were cutting.
No.
They were sitting there and they were -- they were --
Support -- feeding each other.
Yes, they had a feeling there's a kinship there.
Yeah, yeah.
I've heard him play. I've heard him play once when he was with Stuff.
Yeah, that's when I'm talking about.
I heard them on 52nd Street, I know. And I heard them play together, it was wonderful --

Yeah, listen I want to explainmyself right now on that. When I said compete, I wasn't intend -- speaking of a sense of contest of any kind. What I meant was that he -- that he -- that was -- he was equal, he bought the same amount of the -- they were in the same class, that's what I mean, when I said compete --
Oh, yes. Yes.
I meant that you know -- sometimes a guy will be left behind or something. That's what I meant, you know.
Well I see that. Because I've seen it a lot in musicians, that're greater than many of the others, and I've seen him be very kind.
Yeah.
I have.
Yeah.
I'll give you one instance. and I went to a concert, Jazz at the Philharmonic on the Coast --
Ted Farlow California
Yeah.
Maybe this has no purpose right here, except that it might -- it might.
Well, it's nice to hear anyway.
But I saw Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich.
Yeah.
And the same thing, they're both drummers.
Yeah.
Now they both had different spots, they both played with different groups, all this sort of thing.
Yeah.
They were passed around as the two drummers. But the one thing they both played. Now I know that Buddy has far superior technique --
Yeah.
-- and yet it was a wonderful thing that happened between those two drummers. He never once said, took like what Gene did and doubled it or tripled it --
Yeah.
-- which he could've done.
Yeah.
-- you were -- I know -- knowing Buddy,
Put him down.
-- I know that he was capable of that.
Yeah.
But it was just a wonderful, admirable --
Yeah.
-- time between the two of them.
Yeah.
And I respected that so much.
I thought that --
-- and it hit emotional heights on account
of that.
Yeah.
Where if it had been the other way, the whole thing would've been lost (unintelligible).
Yeah, oh, I couldn't agree more. I couldn't agree more, yeah, yeah. It's how it should be, it's not a battlefield.
No.
It's a thing of -- love and --
That's right, and emotion.
-- and something wonderful.
And you'd portray it to something. If somebody --
That's right.
-- comes in, if somebody comes in and you'd play, and you'd say, oh I enjoyed it -- it's a happy thing --
Yeah, sure. That's right.
Of course it's emotional -- jazz, that's a big part.
Yeah, yeah.
But I think that by the same reason, they say who's your favorite -- who's your favorite. I say, well I don't have none.
Yeah.
I can hear Bunny one night and I hear Jonah one night and I hear --
Yeah.
-- somebody else the next -- Louie the next night, I might enjoy all three of them, or hear them a week apart.
That's right. That's right.
And the night I hear Bunny I might think he's the greatest I ever heard.
Yeah.
And he might be playing good, and yet I might hear him two weeks later and he's not playing good.
That's right.
So you've got to be wide open.
I mean the thing is that what it is is you love the music and everybody and anybody can produce something that is moving to you and you're grateful to them and you love them for it and that's it.
Thats right.
I know.

But by the same token, I don't think that -- that people should...they say, oh, somebody is currently playing -- they have a record or something and they think that's the greatest and they think anything he does is the greatest. That's not always so.
No.
That isn't always so.
No, of course it isn't.
They aren't open-minded at all.
No.
I'll tell you a very incident with Woody Herman and I one time --
Actually this is quite a bit -- what we're talking about now is a -- an interesting subject, topic --
Right.

-- that we ought to comment on. You know when I said to you I had somequestions and thoughts worked out in case we had time, we'd talk about it. Well this is one of those sort of topics. There're things --
Yeah.
-- to talk about here and so let's stay with your life story, first --
Okay.
-- and we'll do that -- and then we'll get on this broader subject of the music itself.
Okay, you ask me -- where shall I go now?
Yeah. Well, let me see now. Just a second, I'll switch off. Now, Red, just in order to keep everything in order, you talked about being with the Flaming Youth Revue --
Yeah.
So then what followed that?
Well, after that I don't remember how long I was, that maybe a year or maybe two years --
Yeah.
Might be two years. I don't know. But during that time I was doing solos with that thing. With that group.
Yeah.
I'd go out and do solos and different type of solo, I was getting away from the -- well other things I was doing, I was trying to be more jazz -- and they were Accepting it a little bit.
Yeah.
They would let me do it -- the producer would -- so after that, that kind of disintegrated.
Yeah.

And so we decided that I should do a single. And there was few bookers that were interested. So, Jack Tiboo knew some people -- Paul Ash, that booked Paul Ash, and they came in to see me with the Revue and they said maybe -- he'd be a good single, because a solo -- xylophone act was a good thing to have in a number two spot on a vaudeville bill, it may be eight acts --
In the number two?
You see -- yeah, well vaudeville acts were pretty well set in the type of thing they'd have.
Yeah.
IN other words, they'd have an opening act, which could be anything from a skater to seals --
Yeah.
-- to anything.
Yeah.
-- now the second act is usually a single act.
Yeah, I see.
Not -- now it could be -- usually if the comedian -- if there was a comedian on the show --
Yeah.
They would have the number two act -- would be a musical act.
Yeah.
But if Sophie Tucker was on the bill, they might have -- a little single comedian in that spot, see?
Yeah.
So it depended on -- so when the -- when they would book the theaters, they'd book all these things in mind, you see?
Yeah.
Now maybe but the Flaming Youth Revlew,
we would opening the shows a lot of times, see?
Yeah.
Other times, certain theaters, we might be closing the show.
Yeah.
Follow?
Yeah, I do.
It's all who's on the bill. So, a musical act in the number two spot was good.
Yes.
To come out and do maybe 12 minutes --
Yeah, yeah.
Real fast thing, get off with the band-- rumpty-rum-rum and you're off.
Yeah.
It gives them a chance to change the stage, backstage.
Yeah.

So anyway we went to the thing and the guy heard us and so he said, well there's an opening with Paul Ash, for the opening show at the Oriental. So, I -- he booked me on it. Now Paul saw me and he okayed the idea that we'd try a solo with him and that's the first time I did it with a band.
With a band.
And it had a good band --
And Paul Ash had a name then?
Oh, yeah, but he had a great band. Yeah, he had people like Art Clayfield, and -- on drums -- good -- good jazzmen in that band.
Yeah.
It was a romping band. I remember we had George Washington, a singer -- George Gibbet, Frankie Banier, Little Watson, all these young people.
Yeah.
And he promoted them. And in the second week they had Ruth Edding.
OH, NO kidding?

We copied them and give them back to him. Charlie had a few, we had some nice charts. So we went up there and I swear the people in Bar Harbor no idea what we were doing. No idea what we were doing.
Oh dear.

So, we didn't mind, we just enjoyed the band, we really enjoyed it. Rented two houses, and we lived in the -- they guys lived in the houses, and finally Mildred came up, and we rented a house and we had a wonderful -- we had clambakes on the beach on our day's off and it was just a great time. So, 4th of July came around, and that was the big time for Rudy Vallee to make his appearance at Bar Harbor in the same ballroom. So, naturally we have to go on first. And, we barrelled, I mean that band really played. And we

finished and there wasn't too much applause, except as I walked off the stage, Walter Gross and Mickey Bloom were standing there and they were telling Rudy Vallee, 'If you think we're going to go on after that band, you're crazy.'
How funny.

Walter and I used to laugh about it cause he remembered it, so they waited about 20 minutes -- course he was a great hit, Rudy Vallee -- wonderful in those days and -- the band -- he had a good band, but it was just that complete different approach to music than this band --
Sure, sure.
Guys like Herbie Haymer and Tony Zimmers were standing up and really blowing -- they were playing.
Yeah.
So when we came back from that panic it was really panic, Mildred finally -- she went back to Forest Hills for awhile, then she came up and I said, SOS, we're in a panic up here. So we came back --
Had they paid off or --

No, the guy started not paying us off after July 4th, I don't know he was -- and we didn't have any money, we were fishing for flounder and taking -- Neal Reed was baking apple pies and we were eating flounder and applie pies just for days. The guys were -- so, we finally got them started coming back to town.
Yeah.

So then that winter, it was that winter? Yes, I think it was that Fall. They opened the Famous Door and they wanted me to go in there. With the band. Now Mildred had worked out in Detroit with Irving Aaronson's Commanders --
Yeah.
There was a couple of guys that I'd met, Stewie Fletcher and Tony Zimmers was in that band, a lot of guys --
Stewie Fletcher, trumpet player?
Yes.
Yeah.
So he was in New York, he'd just graduated from Yale, I think, and he was a very good friend of Louis's -- Armstrong's --
YEAh.
He was interested in music --
Yeah.
He really wasn't serious about it.
No.
So they wanted me to go in the Famous Door. Now I really didn't want to be a leader. I never did want to become a leader --
Didn't you?
I never had aspirations to be a leader.
It was just a means for me to play what I wanted to play, I think.
It worked out that way.

Yeah, and I wasn't going to go into 52nd Street. So I didn't want to go in with the usual Dixieland band, but most the bands up to that time, played Dixieland, when they had seven pieces or six pieces --
Yeah, the smaller bands.
Yes.
Yeah.

Oh, so I said, 'My, there must be a different way.' So I started to think, there's got to be a different way to do it than that. So I said, why have drums, or why have piano. We don't need it. Maybe the horns will be enough harmony. I was still -- I was playing xylophone.
Yeah.
And so I formed a band with no piano, or no drums. We had Dave Barbour on guitar, and Pete Peterson --
Yeah.
And I got Stewie Fletcher --
Yeah.
-- and Herbie Hart and Don McCook on clarinet and myself. Just six of us.
Yeah.
So we played, like riffs --
So tell me again, you had Stewie on trumpet --
Yeah.
And Herbie --
On tenor --
Yeah --
Clarinet, Don McCook, he was just playing ed clarinet.
Yeah.
And bass and guitar. No piano or drums.
Yeah.
And it swung, wonderful.
Yeah.
And we played the Famous Door, Teddy Wilson played in between.
How about -- as a single?
What?
As a single?
As a single, he was starting as a single.
Yeah.
And it was a very -- right beside (unintelligible) and Leon and Eddie's, and 52nd Street, and the band was a -- just turned out to be a real sensation.
Well that would be about the first time that anybody would be playing -- were you playing vibra-harp
No, playing xylophone.
You were playing xylophone and that would've been the first time that -- that Jazz xylophone would've been exposed like that, in a place like that, in New York.
That's right, to that extent.
Yeah.
With a small group like that.
Well nobody --
What?
Nobody else was playing jazz xylophone were they?
No, nobody, no. Nobody. There was nobody on that instrument at all. But, that's what they wanted.
Yeah.
And I thought it was a great idea and we got -- the more we played we got more prolific on it. Gee this got to be good.
Was -- did you have arrangements worked out?
Yeah, we did head arrangements, just worked on head arrangements.
Oh -- oh, yeah.
And we were there quite -- oh, quite awhile and oh -- everybody used to come along. I remember first time
that was thrilling (unintelligible) to me was that Bea Lillie and Reggie Gardiner was in a show --
Yeah?
And they came in, my picture was out in front --
Yeah?

And they came in and they said, 'In a Mist.' And I have to tell you this story about that before. But it was true and they fell in love with the band, they used to bring Hyde -- Johnny Hyde in -- End of III - side 1
Well what --

So they came in -- they used to come in quite often and listen to the band. So then we got so, that Winter, that the kids that were going to the Stork Club, on the other side of Fifth Avenue, got interested in jazz, and they started to coming over from the other -- east side over to west side, which is --
Oh, really?
-- right across Fifth Avenue --
Yes?
And yes, they got real interested in it.
No kidding.
So most of that Winter we stayed there.
And the band was quite a nice thing?
Yeah.
Was Mildred working anywhere, was she doing singles, dates, or anything at that time?
Oh, she would go in and out of town before that, yeah, she would make dates out, she'd go up in the theaters in the midwest --
Oh, yeah.
And she'd go to theaters maybe in Chicago.
Who was booking her? Do you remember? Who was the booking office?
Gee, I don't know. I think -- I don't know whether it was CBS -- Columbia Artists Bureau or something like that.

It doesn't matter, I was just wondering.

OH.
Who handled Fred Waring.
Please -- oh.
And he just was a -- love thing -- he and his wife both adored Mildred's singing and --
Yeah.
And she just would up handling her.
So he sold her and Willard Robeson on the a Vick's Program which was quite a nice program for awhile.
Oh, yeah.
And then he booked her -- he booked her out in Detroit during that time, and different things --
Yeah.
And he kinda helped me out.
Oh, that's good.
And --
Well all right, I didn't want to sidetrack you, go back to:
She was working out well, she -- we were living in Forest Hills, I used to drive out every night and --
Yeah. Had you bought that house? You -- you were renting it, had you bought it?
Yeah.
Really?
We decided to live here, which is the way it is. why I did.
Yeah.
We decided to live here, but actually Mildred really wanted to go back, go to California --
Yeah.
And I wanted to go back to Chicago.
Yeah.
So we just --
Just stayed there.
-- neither one of us gave in, more or less
Yeah.
I didn't know California and she didn't think Chicago -- that much at that time.
Yeah.
She liked New York -- we got so we both liked New York.
Yeah. And New York was the center of things --
Oh, it was a wonderful city then.
Yeah.
And it was an exciting city then.
Yeah.
Everything --jazz was starting to come in.
It was coming into its own.
Yes. And so -- after that we moved down to the Hickory House.
Yes.
Next job.
Yeah.

With different groups and different things. Dave Barbour and I and Pete Peterson, maybe a drummer sometimes maybe not. We used to play what they called race records in those days, butchered blues, and Thelma White and all --
Yeah.
-- these things --
Yeah.
-- I used to play real funky style piano --
Really?
-- and Dave would wang on the guitar --
Was this for Dave Capp, up at Decca?
Yeah. Dave. Yeah.
Yeah.
And Dave even tried to change my name back to Kenneth Norville on a couple of records -- do you remember that, ' Decca Stomp ' and some of those, he changed it, yeah.
Confusing.
But by the time we were in the Hickory House, it was really jumping. We were sounding good.
Yeah, yeah.
Everybody used to come in a listen to the
band. It was a really unusual type thing, because it was a small band, that was really different.
Yeah.
It was interesting to me, because to see what we could get going --
Yeah.
-- and it happened.
Yeah.
It happened emotionally, too, cause -- which was good and Herbie played good, Stewie played good, Dave Barbour was playing good. No amplified bass or guitar --
Yeah.
Just string sound and we played, very, very soft and very light.
Yeah. Yeah.
And the Famous Door, was kind of a nebulous thing, you didn't believe it, all of a sudden it would get to you, people would say, 'You know I'd sit here for an hour, I don't believe the way I feel.'
Yeah yeah.
So then they tried to take us over on the East Side. Worked us into -- Johnny Hyde booked us in the Versailles. And, it wasn't right.
No.
Guy come up and we were so steeped in

playing jazz and we were playing the early set, they had another band that played for dancing and they had Willie G. Howard I remember, and the guy -- headwaiter came up and said, 'Play a rhumba.' And Dave Barbour said, 'What's that?' We used to drive this guy crazy. You -- What's a rhumba? He's a -- he'd say, 'Play a waltz.' 'Is that one, two, three?' We used to say. And, we got out of there --
That didn't last too long.

And about that time oh, MCA said to me, asked me if I'd like to go into the Commodore with a bigger band. Now one of the records we made on Decca was 'Gramercy Square,' which was the first one that Eddie Sauter made.
Yeah.
He made a little arrangement for that, group and played mellophone himself. He had four horns. But --
Oh, yeah.
But de -- Decca was afraid to record without a drum or piano. They just were scared of it, they didn't know what to do with just bass or guitar.
Yeah.
They didn't know how to make that --
Afraid it would be too thin.
Yeah, it would be too thin --
Too light.
It would be topheavy.
Yeah.
Of course, I think nowadays, they'd do it. I'd do it. But I think it was just habit, more or less --
Yeah.
-- that made them think that they can't do it that way.
Yeah, it wasn't the age of experimentation.
No, it wasn't the age of really trying to do it. But even when I had the trio with Cal and Mingus, we had that same problem. They didn't know what to do without drums or piano.
Is that right?
They didn't really ever let that trio record as good as it played, because they didn't know -- how to do it. They'd turn. We had to have a constant thing, which was Mingus --
Yeah.
And they were invariably, if we got strong on top, turn it down. Which would turn him down.
Yeah.
See? So the balance was --
Yeah.
-- and we, as a trio, had a perfect balance all the time. Soft, pianissimos -- or --
Yeah.
Medium Meeting fortes or playing loud. We had it altogether that way.
Yeah.
But it never came out that way.
No.
But getting back to this small group --
Yeah?
Ah -- so we added Bill -- we had I found Moe Purtill Milt Pearl and put him on drums on some of the dates.
Oh.
And Howard Smith, on piano. We added those.
Yeah.
So we did a lot of dates that way. So it But made it a bigger band. when I So went into the Commodore I just added -- we had three saxophones and four brass, four rhythm.
Who were the other brass guys?
Brass was -- let's see, Stewie Fletcher, P Hyland Eddie Sauter and Bill Highland.
Oh.
And Al Mastrum on on trombone.
Oh, yeah.
We had three saxophones, we had Herbie Haymer Hamer, Slats Long, and -- let's see Herbie Hamer, Slats Long
and I can't remember who the other one was.
Was it two?
Frank Simiont.
Oh, yeah.
And then we were there most the summer and we went out and the first job that --
Mildred didn't sing with that band at all?
No, no.
No.
We had a male singer. And then we went out and did a few dates, like Groton Point, around after we left at the end of the summer.
This was where we are, Groton Point?
I know. I know that.
Did you know that?
We used to play out there with the band some.
No kidding, and --

We came out of the Commodore after the summer, it was early Fall. So we played a few single one-nighter's there. Everybody was wrapped up in the band. And that's when I started Eddie writing just sax backgrounds and so many tunes were coming out that Stewie or somebody would learn the melody and he'd write a sax background. That's when
Eddie started writing arrangements.
Yeah.

So now they got me a job at the Syracuse Hotel. So we had -- added a little girl singer, Nancy Flake. And the boys -- we didn't keep the boy, we kept the girl. So, Slats Long -- his wife worked the Roxie, so he wanted to stay in town, so he said he'd go up till I found somebody. Now we opened, we were a big hit in Syracuse, it was a wonderful thing. Was a great room and the band sounded good, it was soft --
Yeah.
Which was what they wanted.
Yeah.
And so one weekend, we had to work five days there, and I went over to Utica, and heard a kid in a d'Amico club, and I immediately hired him. It was Hank Damico.
OH.
So he came and joined us.
Yeah.

And then we did a few air shows out of there. Remember one that were on at NBC, and somebody in Chicago heard it and told them about it in Chicago. Don Roth came in from Chicago, and hired us for the Blackhawk.
No kidding?
Now Mildred was going to go with me one
way or the other. Finally when they -- finally they said, well we'll put her in the show with Ronald Vincent. With a dance team. Now, we had -- still had the little singer, Nancy Flake --
Oh.
So, when we get to Chicago, we rehearsed the show with Romd Vincent and Mildred and the dance team.
Yeah?
Well we're on the air and Mildred being such a hit in Chicago, with Paul Whiteman during those days and years she was with Paul Whiteman --
Yeah?

-- that WGN got ahold of MCA and Roth said, 'Why not put Mildred on for some tunes?' Cause we were doing maybe 20 or 30 programs a week out of there. We were working -- in those days you worked seven days a week with a Sunday matinee. And she started -- that meant you started -- you worked from 7:00 to 9:00 and 10:00 to 1:30 --
Yeah.
Everyday. That's a lot of hours.
Terrific. Seven days a week?
Yeah, so she went along and we stayed that whole winter, so that's how it got into it, they were on a Purtil thing. Now Maurice Pearl married the girl singer.
Oh.

And Mildred got on and we had no place for her. She -- Mildred still kept her there. In Chicago. And I was -- I guess naive, I didn't know she was going with Maurice, but Mildred knew, I don't know how, but she knew that she was going with Maurice Pearl. And, they got married in Chicago --
How about that?
So after that winter going through, we just naturally -- they wanted to book the both of us, with -- which was perfect for both of us, we both wanted it.
Sure. Yeah, it worked out marvelously.
So that's how it happened, we become --
Yeah.
-- working together.
That's when the --
In other words, you had no plan of it, it just developed.
No, it came about.
Yeah.
And that's when they dubbed King -- Queen, Mr. and Mrs. Swing.
Mr. and Mrs. Swing, yeah.
Yeah.
And I think Benny Goodman did the first --
Red, I don't want to interrupt you, but

Well it was a very soft, subtle type of swing. We didn't have a heavy drum or anything. And I realized what the band that I'd had on 52nd Street, that the instrument that I played, the xylophone, didn't have the loud, screeching potential that a trumpet or a trombone or a clarinet or a tenor or an alto would have. I'd have to approach the music in an entirely different way which I found in the sextet that we had. And that's what I tried to carry over in the band cause it had the same -- same approach to the instrument --
Yeah.

-- but it's -- during that time in Chicago , I found I tried to use marimba and I even tried to use vibraphone in a couple of the situations. But with the saxophones it didn't quite jell at that point. The marimba was too low, was down in the pitch of the saxophones --
Yeah.
Where the xylophone was an octave higher, which kept it out of a more of a solo thing,--
Yeah.
And all I did was play solos, so I wasn't part of the band, so it wasn't necessary to change any of this.
No.
So, we did try to keep the style from
the small band over to the big band.
Yeah.

So now Eddie Sauter was writing pretty well, and he was doing some great arrangements for Mildred, also some good things for the band. And the guys were very enthusiastic about it. One thing he did, which we had talked about, was that we were trying to write for the individuals and not just write band arrangements.
Yeah.
We studied each man. We wrote things for Stew Pletcher, --
This is what Ellington always did, was write for the guys.
Yeah, and I rewrote for Hank d'Amico, which he --
YEAH.
-- played such a great clarinet sound, wood sound --
Yeah.

-- and Frank Simone had such a great lead alto, he was a great lead alto man. And, we --we tried to grab all these things and utilize them. Another thing we did is we tried to write linear into the thing so that the third alto would be just as interesting as the first alto in playing the part, in the motion of it.
Hm.
And he started to study that. I got him a teacher and he absorbed and he did very fast. And it started to turn in that direction.
YEAH.
It started to --
Yeah -- that was your own thinking for him --
Yeah, it was my think -- yeah.
Yeah.
-- and to this day I get musicians that were listening in those days, how they used to stay up and listen to that band on the radio.
To see what you were doing.
Their favorite -- oh, what a band -- and -- but I realized, too, that it wasn't people's conception of what Swing music could be --
No.
-- they thought that it should be loud and
YEAH.
-- it should be boisterous --
At that time, I mean that was the fashion then.
At that particular time -- they weren't aware of anything like that except --
No.
-- the heavy, --
Yeah --
-- bass drum type of --
Yeah --
-- and the flagwavers and things --
Yeah.
And playing very loud.
Yeah.
And, actually, I imagine a couple of dates that we did after leaving the Blackhawk, we were very popular on the campuses though, in the colleges they loved it.
Yeah.
But some of the other little places around Chicago, they say, well when are you going to start to swing?
Yeah.
And we probably have been waiting for a half hour, but they didn't --
It was too subtle for them. Yeah.
And since then, I think possibly the band was just about five years too soon. It'd been better if it had been just a little later --
Yeah.
At that time.
Yeah, that's right. You were breaking ground, actually?
At that time with that sort of band, it was, yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Because at the end of that engagement there, that's when Basie came in -- into the Grand Terrace --
Yeah, that's right.
-- that's when he was forming the band.
Yeah.
And, -- and we were there when they were forming the band, we used to go up to the Grand Terrace then- Earl had left. (unintelligible).
Yeah.
Basie was in there. And, I don't know, it's -- it was -- it was a thing that we finally had to have a few arrangements to end this -- maybe the intermission with we'd play a couple like that.
Yeah. Yeah.
But I remember we went up to the University of Wisconsin, and they just thought it was wonderful and they -- they stood and cheered us for the things that we did, you know.
Yeah. Yeah.
They enjoyed the musical part.
Yeah, the kids were listening more at that time.
Yes. And, of course, with the musicians the band was very popular.
Yeah.
More so with the musicians.
Yeah.
Very much so.
Yeah. Yeah. Well --
So then we went to the Coast and it developed pretty well. It was an enjoyable job. We worked awfully hard, Though, awfully hard. It was very nervewracking working those hours.
Were all the jobs those long hours all the time?
IN Chicago, all the time, seven days a week. There was no day off in those days.
No.
Seven days a week.
Yeah, that's awful tough.
That's pretty rough, you stay nine months -- you stay nine-ten months in a club --
Yeah.
-- like that and a matinee Sunday --
Yeah. Yeah.
And then make out program, my goodness, you have to make 30 programs a week, some of them 15, some half hour --
Yeah, on the air all the time --
-- course it was -- in those days, that was, commercially, the life-blood of a band, was the air time.
Yeah, I remember.
Sure.
I mean, you've never been able since -- no one ever gets that exposure has -- or has had exposure like that, and after that.
No.
You know?
That's true. But I think that --
I mean that made a lot of bands, like that made Earl Hines band at the Grand Terrace --
Yeah, I think that -- that the style -- all the things that I've done in music, I've been dictated by -- by the instrument.
Yeah.
I think it has to be.
Yeah.
And, even after that, when I --after that band broke up, I went to things that were comfortable for
the instrument.
Yeah.
Now, I mentioned it in a news story, I must say this, early -- in the early '30's, I'd made a few records for Jack Capp, up at Brunswick --
Yeah.
They were tinkly little things, --
YEAH.
-- I tried -- he wanted me to do --
I'm going to hold this off, just a second.
There we go. Red, you were going to tell me, you had something to tell me about -- In a Mist, hadn't you?

-- Brunswick, --

-- but I think it went to --

-- Gene Krupa --

-- I think she used Bunny and Johnny Hodges --

-- the story about --

-- it has no consequence -- now we're up to the point where we're back in New York with the other band --

-- we're in the Commodore --

-- and then we were on the road a lot, and everything, and Mildred wasn't feeling well.

-- and were down in Memphis and we worked all the time.

-- like we were working in those days --
You have to have a break.
-- it isn't good.

Because --

But we'd have it off in some place that you really didn't want a night off --
Yeah, yeah.
I don't know I think it's --
It's a bit too hard.

Yeah.
So we came back, kind of got the idea that Mildred may be -- she wasn't feeling well anyway --

And the doctor said she really shouldn't -- she should take it easy.

Well, I'd formed another little band --

And I tried to break my contract with MCA --

And I went up to Boston and worked for Cy and formed another band, which I had -- I formed a 10-piece band.
Um.
-- which was kind of a -- with Conrad Gazzo Gazzo and Rusty Dedrick Dedrich, and it was kind of a nice band, it was kind of a challenge with three brass and three saxes -- three rhythm.
Different.
Linda Keene was singing and just to try and do something with that.

And it turned out it was a very ---
Well did that --
-- wild, singing band. It was -- we'd play opposite big bands in Atlantic City --
Yeah?
-- really -- we had a good rhythm section, it swung, I forgot all the guys, but they were -- they were a happy bunch of guys, they really enjoyed playing.

And I -- it was very good. Then, I got into bigger -- added a few more, later. And --

-- oh, I don't know, she made some with Eldridge well, Teddy and Roy Albers and the woodwinds --

-- she made 'All The Things You Are,' and 'Fools Rush In' and --

-- and she made some more like that. She was making records every once in awhile -- yes.
Yeah.

-- and after awhile when I'd -- I'd get most of those guys -- I had Barney Galbreath and a bench in that band and I still wasn't satisfied with it, so I really got away from MCA at that time --

[Kent Close] New York --

Oh.
Acetate thing.
Really?

That's what I thought. Where did you --
Then --
-- come across them?

Well, actually how that came about was just before that, after I broke up with MCA, I was deciding what to do, I had a little group at the Hickory House -- with Aaron and, you know, some more people -- Remo Palmieri, (unintelligible) and Ned Williams came to me and said, that William Morris, Jr., wanted me to get a band department. He wanted Duke Ellington and he always liked the band that I had in the '30's, so
he wanted me to get a big band. So I did. I got -- I formed a band. Five woodwinds and six brass. And three rhythm.
Um.

And with that 10-piece band we had, we played down in Dallas and I'd met a kid -- a fella there that was going to Julliard when I was playing at the Commodore. Mildred and I were. So I said if I decide to to get the big band, I was trying to make up my mind whether it was a good move or not --
Yeah?
I said I'd like for you to be the arrangement, because at that time Eddie Sauter had gone with Goodman and doing some very wonderful things. Like Benny Rides Again, and that band.
Yeah.

And I didn't think that he'd be available. So, Johnny Thompson was his name and he was getting married and he was going to California on his honeymoon and suddenly he read in one of the trade magazines that I was forming a band, so they changed their mind and came to New York. And walked in this first day of rehearsal, I nearly fell over. And, he started to write for that band. So, Eddie did a few things; Alec Wilder did a couple of things --
Yeah, I was going go -- to ask you.
The book was very, very good. The book was a very fine book.
Well just --
And we played Blue Gardens and we did Mildred joined us and we did theater dates with Jimmy Durante. For about three or four months.
Because I remember that -- some of the things that Mildred was singing, out at -- Alec Wilder had done the arrangements. So was that the time?
Well I think he did a couple of woodwind things with Teddy and Roy Eldridge, we're on, remember he had a -- I don't know what date that was. I think he did "All The Things You Are," I'm not sure.
Oh, yeah.
Eddie Sauter did most of those, but I don't know what --
Well it was --
Well I know he did a couple for Mildred at that time.
Right.
But he did some for this band, special material things.

band that's on that record. MS. VANCE: Oh, I see. MR. NORVO: And, it was an amazing record, when you think that the record ban was starting that day and we did -- Mildred had did five shows with a cold at the Paramount and so hoarse she couldn't talk. After the Paramount too --
Huh?
After the Paramount -- after the shows --
Yeah, five shows at -- how did -- she did it, I'll never know.
Gosh.

But then we went on the road and it was quite a nice band, it was a great show band, well written and five saxophones and the woodwinds, they all doubled like flute -- we had English horn and oboe -- great rhythms. And then --
How about that?
-- six -- three trombones and three trumpets.
How about that? Did you --
A beautiful band. But then -- we came
-- after this trip we came to a place called The Gardens in upper New York and we began to see that the War was going to draft -- and I started it one by one, this one and this one --
Oh.

And I knew it was going to go, then Willard William Alexander came into William Morris and he said, well you're going to have to cut the band down. Well they'd taken care of all these arrangements and we had a whole book -- so I said, 'I can't do that, it's disappointing, can't we make a go of it.' He said -- 'Well, let me think a minute.' But he finally said, 'No, it's impossible. In this day and age to go -- you got too many men, you have to cut down, to a smaller.'
Get the nut smaller, you mean.

So, I said, 'Well rather than do that I'd just better forget about, it -- cause I'm losing the guys anyway, I don't know it'd be just another band.' So that's when I formed this small group, kept Eddie Burt out of that big band, and -- and Bob Kitsis had been drafted so Hank Kahout was with me, so I took some of them and started this band, played behind Billie on 52nd Street and that's when I formed it. So this was a very successful band. For awhile. Then that started --
Well I guess that was one of the pleasurable times for you, wasn't it?

That was a wonderful little band, we had fun. Shorty was very young, and Shorty was about 17, I think Eddie was 17 or 18, something like that. Young kids. Aaron was quite young, Hank the Kahout Hoop was very young. But it was a swinging band. We were all enthused about it. It's nice to go from those sort of things in music, when you don't go back and have to do the same thing. When you go to something else that's new and try it.
Yes, that is nice.

And they got ideas and you start developing from something like that. But I find if you take six men here and six men there and let them develop they'll be different -looking characters, they'll have a different face -- and each six will look different.
Yeah.
Ca'use the musical will force you to go fortune to go a certain ways.
Yeah.
We did a lot of road work. We went out to Chicago, went out to Rock Island, we went to Detroit, we went to Canada, Winnipeg, we went to Toronto. And we did quite a -- quite a bit of work.
As a leader did you -- did you have headaches, I mean headaches with the guys or --
No.
No, huh?
No, I didn't have any headaches.
No headaches?
With -- you mean with the small band, you mean?
Yeah.
No, no problems.
With the big --

We worked -- we worked and they all enjoyed playing Specs had had experience, they all had experience, he'd been working in Cafe Society -- he worked there -- and I don't know he'd worked for Eddie South, over there on (inaudible) and he was a light drummer, he fitted perfect for that band.
Yeah.
He was --
He was a good drummer, wasn't he?
Yeah. It had a good feel. They were happy to play and they were exhuberant about playing.
Yeah.
It was a nice time.
Yeah, well when you were on the road with the big band, did you have headaches? Management headaches, or travelling --
Well no. What do you call headaches? It's like any business. When you have a business, do you have head-
aches? I mean --
Yeah.
-- you have problems, and why should it be any different with a band, it's a business, after all actually.
Yeah.
It may be a little different, but, actually when you're a leader, all the men's problems become your problems.
Yeah.

They don't know what to do. But you get so that when you hire people, for a band of that sort, they're with you for a couple of days, you know whether they're going to be people that can make the road or not make the road, you know immediately --
Yeah.
-- it's the way they handle themselves.
Yeah.
And you know who -- how they're going to be as musicians, by the way they fall into things.
Yeah.
That isn't such a mystery as it might seem. But headaches? I really didn't look at them as headaches, I just look at it as part of being a leader.
Yeah.
When I guy comes and he says he has a
problem here or that he owes a payment on his house or he this and that and the other thing, you kind of -- you listen to it --
Yeah.
-- and you do what help you can, sure. If he's having problems at home, it's the same sort of thing. You're more or less a father-confessor, they tell you and you try to help them work them out.
Yeah.
A lot of times by listening to them intently they talk them out.
Yeah.
By hearing themselves telling you about it.
Yeah.
I don't look at those things as problems. I think you could make it more problems out of them, if you give a lot of thought to it as a problem.
Yeah. Well some guys don't want to be bothered, you know. It depends what --
Well I think that's true, but I don't think that you're going to get the cooperation --
No.
-- unless you have some sort of interest in the person himself.
That's right.
'Cause, unless they have an interest in you, I don't think that they're going to give you everything that they could give you as a musician.

No. I was going to say, good percentage of your problems are defeated in the fact that the guys are in love with the band. That they love what they're doing and they're are sold. So you got happy guys. Regardless of what things that might be troubling them, basically, they're happy guys and it's a happy group.
Well, I think they are. Because I think anybody -- just like my mother used to say when I was young, she said, 'You know, music's a wonderful thing. You can't play music without being happy.'
Yeah.
And I think that's always stuck with me.
Yeah.
Because it's true, to do it right, you really gotta have a good feeling about it.
Yeah.

And I think that when a fellow has problems, it affects his music, I think you should listen to him and try -- if you can't help him, but I think you should be very frank. He'd rather have you say, 'I can't help you,' than say, 'Well I can -- let me see maybe -- maybe I can.' They'd rather
say, I can't help you, but I'll see what I can do. Maybe I can find something or work something out. Maybe we can find a way out of it.
Yeah.
They're more apt to be -- like that sort of approach.
Yeah.
I find.
It's more straight forward.
Sure, I think so.
Yeah.

And I think everybody has problems, but when you're close together, when you're working close to people all the time, there's going to be -- you've got to learn to get along with people. Especially in the music business.

And a bottle. They had a local band there too, Benny Winestone was in it, I remember, and a few people.

Ah -- we did very well on the Street. I don't know -- people seemed to accept us on the Street.

All the groups I had on the Street seemed to be accepted --

Yes, we seemed to be accepted, more or less.

And then that -- started, we'd lose guys. Then we went on the road and came back and to a place down on Broadway and 48th Street, it was, that's where the Metropole is now, is -- it was a fish place then.

And we opened it and Duke followed us, I think -- that was a good -- then it looked like I was going to lose everything in the Draft, I mean, looked like Shorty was going to go in, and then Hank Kahout to go and Jimmy Rowles Rhodes was coming with me --
Yeah.
-- and then he got drafted, so he had to
go back to California. So he went in a band out there, and then Hank went to Cleveland, he didn't go in, so he stayed in Cleveland.
Oh.
So finally, Shorty was drafted and Aaron was drafted and just worked out that way.
Yeah.

Aaron wasn't drafted, but then we hung around and was doing a few dates and then we formed a -- we went to Chicago with a sextet with drums, bass, piano, clarinet and vibraphone. And we did that for awhile, we had Remo Palmer; we added a guitar to it.
Yeah.
And, then we came back to the Hickory House with them. And that kind of broke up and then during this later period, then, I just jobbed around New York, and --
Yeah.
That's when Goodman called and said he had the Seven Lively Arts and Teddy's band had been formed, Teddy Wilson's band had been forced to break up. And --
Do -- Teddy didn't have that band very long did he?
Who, Teddy?
Yeah.
Oh, it was quite awhile.
Was it?
But he started losing guys and it got to be the same problem.

You couldn't get gas and you couldn't get around -- and you couldn't stay in New York to work, so there's no alternative.
Yeah.
So that's when we went in the show. So, we went in Seven Lively Arts, so we formed a group with Morley Feld and I remember in a month or so Slam joined us. And that was a quintet.

It was a quintet in the show and after -- we did that in August and I think left -- Benny left the show in the Spring, formed a big band.
Well, who was it in the quintet? Yourself,
Morley Feld, Teddy Wilson --
OH, YEAH.
Slam Stewart, Benny Goodman and myself.
Yeah, yeah. I see.
Five of us --
I see.
And then when he formed a big band, he let Bryan Mike Braun played with the -- he liked the electric guitar, and so we added Mike and we became the Goodman sextet.
Yeah, I see, I see. Yeah.
And then after ayear --
How long did that go?
What?
How long did that go?
Oh, --
You know about, was that like a year?
Year and a half --
Year and a half --
-- two years, something like that.
Yeah, so that took -- the War of -- was over by then, more or less.
Yeah, now we're starting -- yeah, we're getting near the end of it --
Yeah.
And fellas like Shorty were coming out of the Service and Gazzo Gazzo was coming out of the Service, he'd been with the Artie Shaw band --
Yeah.
-- other guys were coming -- they'd call me.
Yeah.

So, Benny was set on these guys, so Woody wanted Shorty and he also wanted Gazzo. And I'd had a band for a short while with Flip Phillips and Ralph Burns, Dick Taylor Johnny Blowers, Clyde Lombardi, we were going for Coca-Cola to England to entertain the troops, but it never got off the ground.
