How funny.
So I had a kinmanship with the band from both Flip and Ralph Burns --
Yeah.
And then Shorty and others --
Yeah.
-- so I guess it was just a natural thing that I went with Woody, because he had been wanting me to come with the band --
Yeah.
-- and so finally I said, 'All right, fine.' So I joined him at the Paramount.
Yeah.
And that lasted about a year.

Well, listen while we're on the subject, we might just as well, as I say the fact that this is -- you know not for regular publication, so why don't you tell me -- I was going to ask you anyway, about leaders, and about yourself, that's why I said to you about what headaches and everything, as a leader, well compare how it was working with or for Benny with -- as compared with Woody. Can you do that?
For myself, personally?
Yeah, for yourself, personally.

Well the way I look at it is this way, Helen, it's I used to even tell -- later after I'd worked for Ben and worked for Woody, I worked for them as a side man. And I think from being a leader it made me more alert to things that a leader likes or dislikes.
Yeah.
So of course, having known Benny for years and years and years and great respect for him and all, and yet I worked for him. And tried to work as well as I could.
Yeah.
I enjoyed playing and Teddy did too. And that thing went down everytime -- we played, we tried to be very professional at what we tried to do as well as we could --
Yeah.
Everytime.
Yeah.
And I think Goodman felt that way, too.
Yeah.
Cause I think he was happy with that sextet.
Yeah.
And he always seemed happy with it.
Yeah.
And if we turned it on, it kind of made sense, that land.
Yeah.
It was good improvising, good playing.
Yeah.
And --
I mean, and it was -- I mean the sextet meant a lot to him because the band used to bother him very often, didn't it. And the sextet was a consolation --
Yeah.
-- from the very beginning it was that way, wasn't it?
Yeah. But I think if you've been a leader -- I used to tell fellas later, I'd say if everybody could be leaders for awhile -- it'd be so much better for the leader that they're working for --
Yeah, that's right.
-- cause they'd know the problems and
Sure --
know what was happening and anticipate a little more.
Yeah.
But you can't be -- you can't be wholly selfish in any of these situations.
No.
You can't be as a leader and also you can't be that you gotta please me 'cause I'm a side man --
That's right.
-- or I'm good, the side man.
Yeah.
I think your outlook on the whole thing has got to be very broad.
Yeah.
I did the same thing with Woody. I felt that I did as well as I could with Woody. I enjoyed that band it was a wonderful band, I enjoyed everybody in it.
Yeah.
I loved Bill Harris, I loved Flip Phillips playing, I love Gazzo, I loved all those guys that played --
Yeah.
-- Ralph Roth and Don Lamond (unintelligible).
And there was a wonderful spirit in that band --
Yeah, everybody in that band, the saxophones, and everything.
Yeah.
Mickey Foldus, all these fellas, trombone section was wonderful. The brass was great. Gazzo and Pete Cendoli and Shorty and them --
Yeah.
It was a good brass section and they played wonderful. And they wanted to swing --
Yeah.
-- and they wanted to really do it and it was emotionally good. And --
Would you say that was as good a band experience as you ever had?
That I ever worked with, you mean?
Yeah.
With Woody? Well, I'd say at the time I think it was probably the best band in the country, then. I don't know. Comparisons are -- I s'pose it was --
Yeah.
I s'pose it was. Although Benny had a-- the year before, Benny had a wonderful band.
Did he? Who was in it?
Yes, he did. He had a wonderful band, great players.
Who, can you remember?
Very good band. Yeah, I --
Cootie wasn't in the band, then, was he?

No. He had four trumpets, see he had (inaudible). That's what I used to call them, Gazzo, Fazzo, Muchi and Best. They're our advertising agency, cause they'd stand up and play and it was really something to hear those four trumpets.
Yeah.
And the way that Gazzo got with Benny he called me to know where to go to join Woody, and he called Benny's office and Benny answered the phone and he was on the job at Hartford that night.
How funny.
So he stayed for awhile and then he left and went with Woody. But, --
Well Red, guys in Benny's band were never happy like guys in Woody's band were happy, surely?
Oh, they were happy in Woody's band, that was a great band.
I know, but they weren't that happy in Benny's.
They were proud of that band -- oh yeah they were proud. They were a proud bunch, in that band.
In Woody's or in Benny's?
Woody's Band.
Yes, in Woody's, I know.
Yeah, very happy --
But Benny's never -- I mean, you gotta take personality into consideration.
Well I was never in Benny's band when it was an unhappy band. I don't know why. I was --
Really?
-- no. That big band, after the sextet ah -- Ben and I always got along --
Yeah.
-- I always got along with Teddy, I just loved playing and loved him. And I played well with Morby Feld, and I loved Slam's playing. And I thought the whole -- whole quintet -- or sextet was fun.
Yeah, but Red, that's --
Well that's not -- now when he had the band. I wasn't involved with his band problems.
No, I know.
I was not a part of the band.
I know, I realize that.

Until he went into theaters and where I started to do, 'Gotta Be This or That' -- which was just a number to get us off the stage, which he started up in -- up in a theater in Connecticut here, that was rea -- I wasn't a part
of the band, as such.
No.
I was a member of the organization.
I understand, I understand, you were part of the sextet.
But I had nothing to do with the managerial problems --
No.
-- or what happened with the band and Benny.
No.
He could change 10 days -- guys, It wouldn't have made any difference to me. I didn't play with them.
No.
Teddy didn't either, Slam didn't either.
No, no.
So I really was not a part of that. I know that there's been a lot of talk about him as a band leader at that time --
Yeah, well --
-- I wasn't too aware of it.

Well Red, I'm not saying this in -- in an attempting to be slighting Benny anyway, because you know, I was always very interested in Benny's band, starting with the first one, which I was closely connected with.
I know. I know.

And it was a wonderful band and it kept on developing, but I think the thing -- you know, I always felt sorry for Benny because he's a perfectionist and can't help himself and this is what made things so difficult in his band. I mean he'd give people the ray and everything, but he couldn't help himself.

Oh, I found this with Benny Goodman. Most of the guys that wanted to play all the time, I didn't think he had trouble with in those periods. Those years. I -- couple of guys I know in the band, I recommended to him. That was -- were not the best acting guys, I was a little ashamed that I'd recommended, but they said 'Oh, this music,' and they had a lot of things to think about and they'd slunch over on the band stand --
Oh, yeah.
-- and they really wasn't getting in in trying time to play well.
Yeah. Anybody's going to mind that.
And I think it aggravated Benny, because I --
Yeah.
-- and it would me, too.
Sure.
If I was a leader I'd say, if you want to play, fine. If you don't, then leave.
Yeah.
So when you talk about the ray I think that -- we never had one word in the sextet, we always tried to go down --
Yeah.
-- we played it and he knew it.
Yeah.
We all knew it.
Yeah.
Ah --

No, well that thing I'm thinking about, anyway, Red, that's not quite the same thing, it wasn't so much that any of the trouble that I knew of in the band, wasn't so much the way guys were acting, or anything, but many guys that were working with Benny were scared.
Yeah.

Because nobody was on a par with Benny's talents. And you know that he couldn't help being demanding, because the thing I felt about Benny was, I always felt that Benny never recognized that people didn't have as -- he always thought everybody should be great. Just -- he was great and he didn't think too much of it, really. I don't consider that he was a very conceited guy or anything. He had this great talent, he kind of thought that that's how everybody should have a talent like that. And he'd look at guys as much to say, what's
the matter with you. And they were thinking, My God, I mean, you know, a lot of the guys in the band were scared. Well in the early days they were.

Well I think the conduct the way the band was Woody's band was run a little different. Now if the guys were tired and kind of laid down on the thing, when we walked off at intermission, somebody would say, 'What's the matter, man? Can't you make it, are you -- is it too fast for you or is the pace too much?'
Yeah.
If he had a few too many the night before and didn't feeling like really playing --
Yeah,
-- so in other words that band more or less policed itself.
Took care of itself.
Policed itself, policed itselt I would say.
Yeah.
And it was a proud band.
Yeah.

Lot of bands across the country used to say funny things and we followed a certain band -- don't want to mention names, it's probably unavoidable to mention it, but we followed the band across the country, to California and we

we were playing Tommy Dorsey's ballroom down at Santa Monica, on the pier, and we looked up and there they were, somebody said, "Hey, look who's out there." Well that band, you know you never heard that Herman band play in your life. And these guys when we walked off at intermission, they walked over, really wanted to make friends after that. And, all across the country we'd follow them, we'd been hearing these remarks. So I think it was a pride that that band had, too.
Yeah.
It was -- felt that it was good.
Yeah.
And it was electrifying. We'd get in a theater and the people-- we'd hit those first notes and the people'd just scream.
Yeah. Well you know, you were talking about believing in things, I mean that's --
That's right.
-- I mean that's the essence and that's what it was, wasn't it?
Right.

And in the best days of any great band, I mean the Fletcher Henderson band was the same thing. When a band -- when the time has come for a band, when it's that way and everybody's -- you know, there's a sense that you're really making history, which you are, really, in a sense. You
know you've got a joint thing going that's -- That's right.
-- that everybody's a part of. You know that must've been very enjoyable, I think. What's Woody like to -- to -- to work with?
Oh, I find him very enjoyable to work with. I enjoyed it.
He's a kindhearted guy, isn't he?
Well I was friends with him before, used to be he and he and his wife were romancing when I had a band on 52nd Street.
Oh, really?
Yeah, Famous Door.
Oh, really?
Yeah, Famous Door with a big band.
And -- Well he's -- he's -- his attitude with the band anyway is fatherly, isn't it?
His what?
His attitude with the band is fatherly, isn't it?
Oh, yeah, he was very easy-going, yeah --
You know, I mean like you said you gotta care about your side men.
Yes. I think so, he was very easy and
the band worked easy. He took everything in stride. He's experienced.
Yeah.
Bandleader.
Yeah.
Yes, I think everybody did their part pretty well, in the band, and they wanted to do well. On record dates or whatever it was.
I was going to say and then the band had a lot of hits. Lot of record hits and everything --
Oh, yeah.
-- which is always exciting isn't it?
Yeah, certainly.
Ah, how long were you with them, about?
[End of IV-1]

Okay Red, now I think we've done a little bit of jumping here, you've talked about having gone with Benny and Woody, now during or prior to that time, hadn't you and Mildred decided that you would -- parting of the ways or -- what had happened?
Yeah. Well, that happened -- well during -- before the time that I went with Benny.
Yeah.
Yeah, and I --
You just felt that --
Last place was down at 31st Street, then I moved out of there and I had a -- I kept a place to practice up at the Yoo
up at the Worth Hotel, so I just -- a doctor friend of mine -- I took an apartment next door --
Yeah.
-- during the War so I traded that suite of rooms, which I paid very little for, for that apartment. So I lived there until I went to the Coast after Woody.
Well Red, --
So at that time --
Yeah?
-- at that time I'd met Shorty Rogers' sister --
Yeah.
-- and that's when Mildred and I was living down on -- I think it was 11th Street --
11th -- I was just going to say, 11th Street.
Off of 5th Avenue.
That's right.
Right by the church there.
Yeah.
That brownstone house -- we lived in a brownstone there.
Yeah.
And we'd come down when I had the group with Specs Powell and Shorty and we're going to Detroit and
I just met her ther and she came down with Shorty and Aaron and -- Eddie and Molly and some --
Was she -- yeah.
And I don't know, when I was with Benny I don't know I was walking near backstage and I run into her. And we had dinner, just friendly --
Yeah.
And she said Shorty was in the Service, down in below -- [Virginia] Quantico or someplace --
Yeah.
And we got talking and --
Were she and Shorty close -- good friends.
What?
Were she and Shorty good friends, they were close?
Oh, yeah, oh yeah.
Yeah.
So it just went from there.
Yeah.
And she'd been married, had a child. We got along fine. She was a wonderful woman.
Yeah.
And, so we just -- we got married.
Yeah.
I and I
didn't think much about it and I realized she was just really the kind of person I wanted to be married to.
Yeah, she made you happy and --
Yeah, I had a happy marriage there too. Very happy. Years and years of happy marriage. She understood the music business.
And --
And she was fond of Mildred and Mildred was, I think, was fond of her. She was fond of the children we had.
Yeah.
And I think Mildred really thought it was all right, because --
Well --
-- it worked out that way.
-- I guess Mildred was big enough to -- to know that since it didn't seem to be able to work out for the two of you together --
Yeah --
-- and she loved you, she was glad to see you happy. In essence, she was glad to see you happy. Hard to take --
Yeah.
-- but she was a very loving person and I can understand how she --
Well a couple of years after we moved to California and came back, I was working at the Embers, here.
Yeah?

And the younger ones were quite young. The baby was six months and Portia's a couple years older and Mark was in first grade, I believe. We used to go up to Mildred's farm. Lot of people say, say to Eve, Aren't you -- how do you feel about that? She said, 'Well I'm sure if Red wanted to be married to Mildred he would.'
Yeah.
And Mildred, too.
Yes, right.
But, it's just that simple.
Yeah, straight forward and --
Open about this. I think that's why Mildred liked her very much.
Yeah. Nothing phoney there. Nothing --
No, no. I don't think there was any -- and she was crazy about the children, Mildred was just insane about them.
Well Eve must've felt sorry for Mildred, too. She must've felt sorry about it. Wasn't she?
Well I don't know if she felt sorry, I just think she -- she admired Mildred greatly and --
Yeah.
And -- there was never anything really -- she was a very unusual woman, Eve was.
Was she?
Lot of her friends, here in New York -- she made a lot of friends.
Yeah.
She made friends very easy.
Yeah.
Was nice --
Yeah.
See, she wasn't show businessy in any way more or less. And we had a nice home and I had a very nice -- and I had a very nice family -- and we were very much in love and we were -- great years.
Yeah.
Course, I lost her five years ago, but way I feel is the way she would've felt that I should appreciate the years that I had. And, --
Well, it's --
-- I suppose you can't say why these things ah -- happen -- you just have to accept. The hardest thing in life is learning to accept -- you can't make it happen the way you want it.
No, you can't. It's quite true that --
No, but she knew that I was a musician
that I'd have to go where I'd have to go.
Yeah.
When I was out there working studios and going crazy, when I first went out, she knew that. But she said, I don't think it's worth it. I think you ought to do what you want to do.
Yeah.
Even if you have to go.
Yeah. Be yourself.
Yeah. I appreciated that.
Yeah.

So I used to have to come back to New York to work, because at that time, Joe Glazer was booking me. And I had a sextet with -- who'd I have? Dick Hyman and Della Lowe and Tony Scott, Joe Mangini, drummer and myself.
You had Joe Benjamin?
Yeah.
Oh.

We worked around New York a little bit then I finally decided, looking over the situation in California that the only way I could stay in California was to have a trio. So I talked to Mundell about it and he said, 'Well, I don't know.' I talked with Glazer, he said, 'Oh no, no. No, no. Can't do that.'
Why?

Well he didn't think it was a good idea, he didn't think it was a good idea, trio. I guess mainly because -- any size group that you have going from one to another you have to go into different surroundings, different type clubs.
Oh, yeah.
No a club that'll support a trio, doesn't -- won't support a sextet.
Yeah.
And a club that'll support a sextet, is more apt to hire eight pieces or 10 pieces, than they would a trio.
Yeah, right.
And if you're a trio --
And he felt that --

-- if you're a trio, and you play opposite maybe you're playing opposite a 10-piece band. So if there's any dancing with drums and all the things that might have any advantage you're at a disadvantage.
Yeah.
So you really have to find the spots. So it's really an economic thing of being billeted where you're supposed to go.
Yeah.
Like if you play dancehall, doesn't make
any difference if you have 10 or 15.
That's right.
If you're doing the job.
Yeah.

So I met the fella that -- he came in to (unintelligible) see me at Marco's Pub last evening -- Lee Gruber, went down to his place in Philadelphia, Joe said all right, I'll book you for two weeks. And, Mundell and I and a bass player went down. And it was -- an awful experience, no drums and no piano, I just felt naked, I didn't know what to do, behind Mundell when he was playing, it's just an odd feeling -- Felt like half of (unintelligible) you were there.

Well you were used to relying on things and -- and Slim Gaillard worked opposite us down there, but I went along like that for the first week or so, and I was just everynight, I'd go home and think about it and think about it. What do I have to do, what -- I have to solidify the thing.
Yeah.
The vibes are the center of the thing.
Yeah.
So I realized that I have to -- some way I had to coordinate this thing. Well the last three or four days, I found out how to play behind the guitar. Found out how to play comp behind.
Yeah.

Found out what I wanted to know there. Now the other part, I'd have to go around. So we came back to New York and Mandell couldn't go to the coast. So I went over to Billy Reeves' Little Club and I'd heard a trio over there and a guitar player who I liked very much. So when Bell said, 'Why don't you come down Monday, I have a friend and I think you two would get along very well,' so I said all right. So I went down to his place and he was going to cook chicken and I think we were back up --work opposite Duke, place above the Turf, remember that club? I don't remember the name of it. Bop City, I think.
Yeah.
So, in walks this guy and that would be Tal Farlow Talifano, which is the same guitar player from the Little Club.
How funny.

So, he wanted to do it. He wanted to go to California, he'd never been. He liked the idea of the trio. But he had to get out of his job, so I booked in Oshkosh-- now here's a strange story of getting the bass. I heard Red Mitchell over in Jersey, once, he was a young kid, and I thought he had great potential. So I thought of his name and I found out he was living in a certain hotel in New York. So I called there and asked for him. I -- A guy answers the phone, I said, 'Red,' he said, 'Yes.' I said, 'This is Red Norvo,' I explained the whole thing to him, and I hired him. I said, 'Meet me in front

of -- by the side of the Park Central Hotel, and go. We'll go. Just he and I cause Mendell had a job was going to fly out and Tal was going to come out after Mendell -- Mendell was going to stay till Tal got through with his job with the Little Club.
Yeah.

So, we're in a car and he goes to sleep and I'm driving and driving and then I stopped to eat and he said, 'If you want me to drive, I will.' Now when I'd see Red Mitchell a few times before, I wasn't sure exactly how -- it seemed strange, but I wasn't sure. I'd seen him in a dark club over in Jersey. I knew his name and the way he sounded. So, this guy went along, and we got out, just about to Chicago and I said, 'Hey, Mitchell.' He said, 'Mitchell? My name's Red Kelly.' I'd hired the wrong Red. So we went on to -- from there went to Columbus and went on to Honolulu for -- we played over in Honolulu for about four months. And that's where Tal and I really got things together.
Now we came back to town, Los Angeles, and they'd booked us into a club out in the Valley, oh a funny hat place -- So I didn't want to go in there --
Yeah.

-- so that night we went around and we found this -- we went around the clubs and we went to this Haig, which was across from the Ambassador, I said, 'this is the place for us.' So I said to Tal, I'm going to wait until I get this
one. He said, "I don't blame you." So they finally -- Erroll Garner'd been in there. So they finally said okay to put in it. They'd always said -- had just single piano players in there.
Oh.
So I went in and Red Mitchell was not happy with the trio, he was a big band bass player.
Well when did you get hold of Red Mitchell.
OH, I mean Red Kelly.
Oh, you mean Red Kelly.

And it's a good thing we did, cause Red Mitchell got sick right after that, he got tuberculosis right after that, he didn't play for a year or so. So, get back to the story about how -- when Billie Holiday, after I'd moved to California, from New York, Woody broke up, I came back to New York. I was very unhappy here. It wasn't the New York that I'd known in the '30's or the early '40's, at all. Cause I'd been travelling with Benny for a year, and out of town with Woody and being out of town, and it just was a horrible feeling, I walked down the street, see everybody was geniuses in the music business, the feeling that something was gone. I don't know how to put my hand on it.
Had that gone into the '50's?
Well this was in --
Yeah, go --
I went to California in '47, this was '47, '46, and first of -- January, '47.
Yeah, the end of the War --
Yes.
Yeah.

And I know there was Leonard Jean, and I went and Jane and Eve and I went someplace, and I don't know the whole atmosphere of the thing was changed. So I said, to Eve, I'm going out to California. I'm -- we'll see. So I went out, and I stayed with a friend of mine out there, and I said, "Yeah, I like it here," so I -- came back and got Eve, we went out there. Now I didn't have nothing, and we lived in Santa Monica where I lived -- and I still live there. And, now when I was living there in this first period, that Joe Glaser used to call me and I'd get a band for Billie Holiday.
Oh.

And I got some good bands, she'd work at Billy Berg's and we'd go to San Francisco and we made trips to St. -- up and down the coast. So the first date was Billy Bergs and I had Jimmy Rowles on piano, Barney Kessel, Iggy Shevack, trumpet player -- Neal Hefti --
Oh.
And Taylor on trombone.
Yeah.
Saxophone player, oh, Herbie Steward.
Oh.
It was a nice band, we played wonderful.
Yeah.

So we went from there up to San Francisco, and from San Francisco, we did a series in one night. Now in San Francisco, Iggy Shevack, had to come down the court. Eddie Bender was getting divorced or something, he told me the night before he was supposed to be down. He said, 'I'm supposed to be in court tomorrow.' And I said, 'Well you'd better go.' He said, 'Well what'll you do?' I said, 'I don't know.' So I'm standing in front and a fella said, 'You looking for a bass player?' I said, 'Yeah, I need one tomorrow.' He said, 'I know one.' I said, 'Can he read?' He said, 'Sure.' I said, 'Well, send him in.'
So he sent him in, this fella made the rest of the two of them, Iggy never came back. So he made all the one-nighter's with us.
Who was it?
Charles Mingus.
Oh.
So now after I went back to New York --
Well how --
-- and got the trio, and came out, after I had that --
Yeah?

I went back and did the dates with the sextet in New York and when I came out, I went to Honolulu for four months, I came back, I went in there, Red wanted to leave to go with Charlie Barnett, so I had another bass player, so Jimmy Rowkes came in. He was in that band with behind and Billy. So Jimmy was setting there he said, "You having trouble finding a bass player, aren't you?" I said, "Yeah, I can't get the right one." He says, "You remember that fella who worked with us on the tour with Billie Holiday?" I said, "Yeah, How about him?" I said, "He'd be perfect. I don't know where he is, I don't remember his name." I said, "Yes, I do remember his name. I have it home."

So I started calling San Francisco, the union, and I called and and called and finally found him carrying mail in Los Angeles, he wasn't playing. I contacted him, he didn't really want to -- know if he wanted to come or not, he did though. And, oh he was just up in the air all the time, but he was the answer.
Well --
So that was just -- he stayed with us there, we were there about six-eight months on that job. And that's when the trio started to really go.
Well Red isn't that a funny thing, I mean that he did the rest of that Billie Holiday tour with you and -- and you didn't even remember his name. Was he so
I mean it'd been out of my mind.
Oh, I understand -- I mean was he so --
I can't remember, I mean I have a lot of fellas, I mean I worked with you in Boston, when I needed a sub. I don't necessarily remember their names.
No, no.
Because the -- because Mingus is known nowadays, is no reason I should've remembered Mingus in those days.

No, no. Really, what I'm asking you about is, was Mingus that -- was he young then, or was he inexperienced, or was he -- in the cloud or what? No? It just -- he just had come in to fill a -- fill a --
He wasn't working.
Yeah.
And he was carrying mail, so --
Yeah.
Came back and he was rusty.

He used to say, 'I don't think I can do it. I don't think I've been playing enough.' And we said, 'Oh, don't worry about it.' Well it's the same way with Tal when he came with me. Tal used to quit every night. Said, 'I can't play that fast I can't play like you do. I can't it, I'm not used to playing that tempo.' I said, 'Tal, as a trio, we

don't have drums, or any -- any volume control, for loudness or softness so we've got to use speed to -- to do the things -- we got to use other devices to do these. Now to finish the set we've got to use pacing --
Yeah.
We've got to use pacing to govern our sets this way.
Yeah.

So we were in Columbus he said 'I can't.' I said, 'Don't worry about it.' Now we went the four months in Honolulu and we came back and all of a sudden, after Mingus joined us, about a month or so, one night I said, 'My gosh, this guy's playing fantastic.' No problems whatsoever. It -- he was in it.
Which, Tal?

Yeah. Now Mingus always had tech -- but when he got his chops back, and the great think about Mingus is that he had a point on the note, which you'd need if you don't have drums. In other words, the minute he hits that note, it's like a hit.
Yeah.
It's like a stick hitting on a drum or something.
Yeah.
And he had the great point on his note.
You got that beat.
Yeah, well that's the point, that's the point, now not this is a mushy sound, like varoom --
Yeah.
It'd go pooom, it's attack --
Yeah.

Well Tal played the tack with attack and I played it and I made that thing more or less jell without drums and things, but with Minguses laying it down it was great and he played great solo; he had great technique. He was perfect for it. So for three or four years it was great like that. We had a wonderful, I really enjoyed that, we were happy together.
Listen I don't want to harp on it or anything, but a guy that potentially had so much technique in the business? how come he had dropped out, how come he wasn't into this?
I don't know. I never asked him. Really.
No.
Once in awhile he might say things that --
He just got disgusted or --
I don't know, he'd been living around San Francisco, I don't know what he was doing up there --
Yeah. Well that was a wonderful -- he must've been -- thought that was a wonderful, providential thing that -- to go with --
Oh, he was wonderful -- wonderful guy, we
enjoyed, we travelled a lot -- we did different gigs, and everything, go back there.
So you and Tal and he -- made a good personal relationship, as well.

Yeah. Then I had a trio, then Tal hurt his hand, and I had to fill in with that. I tried -- I knew in those days, that was in the early '50's, I knew Joe Pass. But, it was in Vegas and after Tal left. and he couldn't play, he fell through a door and hurt his thumb, so --
OH.
So I didn't know who to get and I was trying, I thought maybe Joe Pass. I'd played up there and I heard Joe.
Yeah.
But he couldn't leave Vegas, I don't know there was some reason, it was a complication of some sort.
Yeah.
So then I thought well maybe I'd better -- Tal had suggested maybe Jimmy Ray, so I got Jimmy Rainey, and
Uh-uh.
Now Mingus had already left, we'd been in New York at the Embers for a coup -- oh, nine -- 12 months, I guess --
Yeah.
-- now when we were at the Embers, after
we left there, that's when Red Mitchell was over the sickness. So he came with us. He wasn't strong. But he joined us and we went out to a place called the Encore.
Yeah.

I told the boss, I mean, "When Red -- if Red gets tired, he's going to walk, he's going to tell me. You know, he's been very sick." He said, "That's fine, Red. I understand," so I said, "Now you've got to build your strength up, slowly, so if you feel that way, walk."
Yeah.
"Tell me, we'll get off for awhile, maybe just five minutes, we'll get back on if you feel like it."
So he built up his resistance and it was great.
That was nice, that was wonderful.
Yeah, it was fine.
Very nice.
So, then when Tal --
Did he get his strength right back?
What?
Did he ever end up getting his strength --
Oh, slowly, it was slow. He built up slow, yes. And he was eating and he got real healthy.
Yeah.
Then, when Tal hurt his hand, then I sent for Jimmy Rainey. And Jimmy came out and joined us.
Yeah.

So I don't know we had a few years of this and then I -- that dissolved, after we were in New York awhile. I went home, Oh, jeeze, I've been working hard, I'll take a little time and I did. And then I met Gene Wright, (unintelligible a guitar player) Bill Dillard, and somebody called me about going to Australia, so -- first thing I know it was suggested that the -- we get Helen, it was great, so we got Helen Humes, and a trio, we went to Australia for about three months.
Oh, I didn't realize that it was just a trio. I thought it was a six or seven piece or something.
No, just a trio.
No kidding?
When we came back we worked around Hollywood for a long time, and then we went in a club, she didn't did something else for awhile, she went back to Hawaii.
Let me interrupt you a second. How did you find Helen as a trouper, to work with any -- and everything?
OH, wonderful. Wonderful.
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah. We had a wonderful time in Australia. She was very popular them and she was very cheerful and easy to get along with.
Yeah. And she's -- she's not ungenerous with her work and I mean she's ready to --
Oh, anytime. We worked hard over there.
Yeah.
We worked a lot of little jobs that were unimportant, but the guy was paying us so much, and he worked us as much as he wanted to. Really didn't realize how much when we went over.
Yeah.
But I enjoyed it, I didn't mind it.
Anyway, Helen had been -- hadn't had so much good work, right up to that time, had she?
No, she hadn't. When -- she was intown there and --
She was glad to go.
-- we became friends and Eve was crazy about Helen and she tried to help, but we just never could get together to work again --
Helen was telling me on --
-- then she moved to -- down south some-place, I think her husband was in the service at the time, or something --
Yeah.
And once in awhile I'd hear from her and it just seemed like -- never quite happened.
Yeah.
And then we came back and Bill Dillard and

Gene and I worked together in Santa Monica during the summer and Bill was killed in a fire, saving another fella. He -- got his head out the window and saved the fella who was sleeping on his couch, but in doing so, he breathed so much smoke that he just lay down on the bed and it poisoned him, the smoke. And the other fella was saved, but they called me in six in the morning and so after that Gene Wright and I couldn't work together

I said, 'Gene, we'll never make it.' He said, 'I know.' So he came to Chicago, or he went to Chicago and then he went back and Brubeck Brubaker, I think at that time, I think it was either Brubeck or Cal Tjader first, and then Brubeck --
For heaven's sake.

But we never worked together after that. We were good friends, and then I -- I -- the guy that we were working for in Santa Monica said, 'I'm not going to get anybody else,' so I said, 'I really don't want to work.' He said, 'Well, I'm not going to get anybody else. When you feel like coming back.' So (unintelligible) called me who's a friend of his and said, 'I'm sorry to hear about Bill,' so I said, 'What're you doing?' I said, 'Let's go over to a place and play some tunes for this guy tonight. I mean he's been very nice to me, I feel a little -- I feel bad, but I feel worse if I -- not at least trying to help him. He's got a club in the -- so Gene had already left and we picked up another bass player, in San Francisco, who was down, and went over and played awhile. And he was
a little scared, he didn't really want to do it, he'd never played in a trio .
Who was he?

Jimmy Wyle, who was with me for years with the quintet. Then we got a bass player, after about two weeks by the name of Red Wooten, who had been with Tommy Dorsey and Woody Herman, and other bands, he was living in California -- and a great bass player and he joined us and I don't know, next thing I know, Lonnie Prozier calls me for the Tropicana, which was open, and so I said sat down, "I'd been up there at the Sahara, and I was unhappy and I didn't want to -- and he said, "Well, I'm having them bring the trio out from (unintelligible), the piano player, and this be you two, and I want you to play softly and play the tunes, nobody's going to bother you. "

So I did and worked all summer there.
IN that -- in that -- I know the place there in that -- in the
Lounge, not the way it is now -- the old way it's first year .
OH, yeah .
And, the other other -- the piano player was well Nierow Bernie -- you know, Peter Nero .
Oh, really?
Yeah . He came out and he lived in Las
Vegas for about three years . Then we came home after LABOR Day and we were working around and -- doing things,, we'd go to San Francisco, and Phoenix with that trio, and --
So you didn't have to work too hard .
We went to Miami, even . We went to Miami , And worked with the trio .
For heaven's sake .
Then came back and Sinatra called us to do a picture . Which we did. So after we finished --
Well don't -- well what was it like, what picture was it?
